places.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. Tempura is wheat-flour battered and deep-fried, and the tentsuyu dipping sauce is dashi/soy-based (wheat-containing soy sauce). Cross-contamination in shared frying oil is highly likely. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
places.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly as a whole: the menu is seafood-centric (live shrimp, fish) and the batter/dipping sauce rely on dashi (fish/bonito stock). Vegetable tempura exists but is fried in shared oil and served with dashi-based sauce, so it is not reliably vegan. A dedicated vegan would need to ask in advance; suitability is not confirmed.

chef_bio.origin: 中京区 富小路三条下る, Kyoto
chef_bio.background: Tominokoji Tempura Matsui opened in 2019 on Tominokoji, just south of Sanjo in central Kyoto, as the namesake counter of chef Matsui Motohiro. Born in Hokkaido in 1977, Matsui first trained as a Japanese (washoku) cook. His path turned toward tempura when he was put in charge of a tempura specialty restaurant in Pontocho, which drew him into the world of Kyoto-style tempura. After honing his craft at well-regarded establishments, he opened this intimate ten-seat counter, where he fries to order in front of guests in a calm, Japanese-inspired room.
chef_bio.philosophy: Matsui pairs the discipline of classical Japanese cooking with Kyoto tempura technique, frying slowly in low-temperature oil to draw out each ingredient's flavor. His hospitality is deliberately unpretentious (kata-hiji harasenai omotenashi) - an easy, approachable counter where he talks through the day's ingredients and pairings with guests.
chef_bio.specialty: Kyoto-style (kyofu) tempura fried to order from fresh seasonal ingredients, carefully cooked in low-temperature oil so each item keeps its own character under a light, crisp coating. The menu changes with the seasons, and the kitchen is known for tempura that eats light rather than heavy. At lunch, the tendon (tempura rice bowl) is a popular draw.

anecdotes.text: Matsui began as a washoku (Japanese cuisine) chef and only moved into tempura after being entrusted with a tempura specialty restaurant in Pontocho, which sparked his interest in Kyoto-style tempura.
He fries Kyoto-style tempura carefully in low-temperature oil so ingredients keep their character while the coating stays light and crisp, served at the counter in front of guests.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hitosara's chef profile confirms 松井基宏 was born in 北海道 in 1977, started in 日本料理, and moved into 京風天ぷら after being 「先斗町の天ぷら専門店を任された」, active at 富小路 天ぷらまつ井 from 2019, with low-temperature frying. Tabelog confirms the Oct 25, 2019 opening and 10 counter seats (席数10席 カウンター10席), seasonal fresh-fried tempura and an affordable lunch donburi.

cultural_comfort.note: A small 10-seat counter where the chef fries each piece in front of you, so some basic Japanese (or a translation app) and comfort with quiet, attentive counter dining will help a foreign student feel at ease.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a tempura specialist: items are coated in wheat-flour batter and deep-fried, so the food is not celiac-safe. A shared frying oil handling many wheat-battered items makes gluten cross-contamination effectively unavoidable.
No dedicated gluten-free fryer or separate-oil arrangement is documented in any source.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tempura is served with tentsuyu (a dashi-and-soy dipping sauce) and/or salt; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and tentsuyu and any dashi base typically include wheat-containing soy and/or other wheat-derived seasonings. Treat the sauces as gluten-containing unless the kitchen confirms otherwise.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetable tempura exists, but the batter, the shared frying oil (used for fish, prawn and other animal items), and dashi/tentsuyu (made with bonito and other fish stock) mean vegetable items are not vegan and carry heavy animal cross-contact. No vegan-specific preparation is documented.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No documented allergy or gluten-free accommodation was found in available sources. The chef does discuss the day's ingredients with guests at the counter, so allergen questions can be raised directly - but confirm any needs in advance.

positives.text: Small ten-seat counter where the chef fries to order in front of you and talks guests through the day's ingredients, making it easy to ask about preparation directly.
Tempura is fried low and light, and is noted as eating less heavy than typical tempura - though this does not change its gluten or animal-product content.

sweep_downgrade.why: The record's own vegan_detail says the shop is 'not vegan-friendly as a whole' and 'not reliably vegan', and its menu file records 0 vegan meals. Every vegetable item goes through the one oil that fries 海老・魚, per the shop's own 夜のサービス天盛 listing 「・海老 ・魚 ・野菜 等」 and a diner's tendon of 海老、鯛、鮭 with the vegetables. 'Limited vegan options' promises a vegan something orderable; there is nothing.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Single-location independent cafe opened in 2015 by owner Mr. Ichikawa, who converted his grandfather's former Kiyomizu-ware pottery workshop (a ~200-year-old machiya) into the cafe. No chain or brand affiliation found.

chef_bio.background: 市川屋珈琲は、京都・東山の清水焼の窯元が集まっていた界隈に2015年に開いた喫茶店です。建物は店主・市川陽介さんの祖父がかつて営んでいた清水焼の工房兼住居で、市川さん自身もここで暮らしていました。築200年を数えるこの京町家はいったん取り壊しの話が持ち上がりましたが、市川さんは『この場所を残したい』という想いから、新築の約4倍という費用をかけて全面改修を決断。京町家作事組の手で、坪庭を望む大きな町家カフェとして生まれ変わりました。市川家は祖父・父ともに清水焼の陶芸家で、兄も焼物の道を継いでいます。市川さんだけは学生の頃から趣味で焙煎をするほどコーヒーを愛し、名門イノダコーヒで18年修業したのち、独立してこの店を開きました。
chef_bio.philosophy: 『一杯のコーヒーができること』を考え抜いた店づくり。市川さんは、来店した人がコーヒーを楽しむうちに自然と美しい器に出会えるよう、『一杯のコーヒーが、工芸への入り口に』なることを願っています。ネルドリップのなめらかで甘い一杯と、清水焼の器が、日常を少しだけ特別なものにしてくれます。
chef_bio.specialty: 看板は、月ごとに移ろう旬のフルーツをふんわりした食パンとコクのある生クリームで挟んだ『季節のフルーツサンド』。果物の見極めや切り方、クリームの甘さの加減まで丁寧に仕立てられ、開店前から行列ができるほどの人気です。コーヒーは店内の焙煎機で日々自家焙煎し、ネルドリップでじっくり抽出。市川屋ブレンド・青磁ブレンド・馬町ブレンドの3種があり、それぞれ父や兄が手がけた清水焼のカップで供されます。市川屋ブレンドのカップは飲みやすさと保温性を考えて縁を薄く底を厚く、青磁ブレンドは香りが立つよう口を広く、と一杯ごとに器まで設計されています。卵サンドやデミオムライスといったメニューもあります。

anecdotes.text: 市川家は祖父・父・兄が清水焼の陶芸家という家系。市川さんだけは学生時代から趣味で焙煎をするほどコーヒーが好きで、自分の淹れたコーヒーを喜んでもらえることに魅力を感じ、名門イノダコーヒで18年修業してから独立しました。
祖父の工房だった築200年の町家が取り壊されかけたとき、市川さんは『この場所を残したい』という想いから、新築の約4倍の費用をかけて全面改修に踏み切りました。
コーヒーは父や兄が作る清水焼の器で提供され、市川屋ブレンドのカップは縁を薄く底を厚く保温性を高めるなど、一杯ごとに器まで考え抜かれています。
看板の季節のフルーツサンドは月替わりで旬の果物を使い、開店前から行列ができるほどの人気。『フルーツサンドのお店』として広く知られています。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 中川政七商店のストーリー記事が、店主・市川陽介さんは清水焼の陶芸家（祖父・父）の家系で兄も焼物を継ぎ、市川さんだけが名門イノダコーヒで18年修業したこと、祖父の工房兼住居だった築200年の町家を『残したい』一心で新築の約4倍の費用をかけ京町家作事組が全面改修したこと、市川屋／青磁（兄作）・馬町（父作）ブレンドを清水焼のカップで供することを確認。co-tripは月替わりの季節のフルーツサンドの人気を裏付ける。2015年開業。

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed Japanese-language machiya cafe popular with tourists; basic Japanese greetings and pointing at the menu will get you by, though staff may not speak much English, so a few Japanese phrases help.

chef_bio.origin: Fushimi-ku, Minamihama-cho, Kyoto — across from Teradaya, near Keihan Nakashojima Station, along the Uji River branch
chef_bio.background: Shimao Coffee opened on May 21, 2023, in a bright, glass-fronted spot in Fushimi's Minamihama district, sitting directly across from the historic Teradaya inn with the Uji River branch flowing just outside. Through the floor-to-ceiling windows you can watch the traditional jukkoku-bune sightseeing boats glide past amid the greenery and seasonal hydrangeas, which gives the room a calm, waterside feel. The café was created by its owner, Oshima, who built it around a very personal idea: he loves the classic Japanese kissaten 'morning' set and wished he could eat it at any hour, not only first thing in the day. That wish became the heart of the place.
chef_bio.philosophy: Owner Oshima's guiding idea is that the comforting kissaten 'morning' should be available all day, not just in the morning — he is passionate enough about morning-café culture that he travels to Nagoya, famous for it, for inspiration. The result is an unhurried, all-day morning experience paired with the changing river view.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the 'Anytime Morning Plate' (いつでもモーニングプレート) served with a drink throughout opening hours — a generous roughly 30cm plate piled with colorful salad, slow-roasted crispy bacon, sunny-side eggs, well-textured butter toast, and yogurt. Alongside it the café is known for its freshly brewed coffee (a deep-roast Bitter Blend and a medium-roast Mild Blend), café au lait, and a rotating selection of cakes, including a distinctive kinako (roasted soybean flour) and bamboo-charcoal cake. Simple plates like butter toast round out the menu.

anecdotes.text: The owner, Oshima, conceived the café around the wish to enjoy a traditional kissaten morning set at any time of day, not only in the morning — and is so devoted to morning-café culture that he travels to Nagoya to experience it, which directly shaped the all-day 'Anytime Morning Plate'.

Set directly across from the historic Teradaya inn with the Uji River branch outside, the glass-walled room looks out on the jukkoku-bune sightseeing boats passing through fresh greenery and hydrangeas, giving a refreshing waterside atmosphere.
A standout among the cakes is a kinako (roasted soybean flour) and bamboo-charcoal cake, served alongside the café's Bitter and Mild coffee blends.

chef_bio.background: Baji Tofu is the work of Kenji Kobayakawa, born in Kyoto in 1960. He came to grilling by an unusual route: he started cooking at 21 in a Western/French-style kitchen, and at 27 took on running a franchise restaurant. In 2006 he opened his own place, choosing yakitori precisely because it is a cuisine that is widely and warmly loved across generations, and wanting to build a restaurant that could be cherished for the long haul. The result is an intimate, dimly lit counter room on Muromachi Street where the light comes mainly from the glow of the charcoal, so the focus stays on the skewers in front of you.
chef_bio.philosophy: Kobayakawa deliberately chose yakitori as an accessible, long-beloved genre in which to test his craft, and his approach centers on freshness and care at every step: chicken bought fresh each day, skewers strung to order, charcoal grilling tuned by feel, and finishing salt chosen with intent.
chef_bio.specialty: Charcoal-grilled chicken yakitori. Kobayakawa sources fresh domestic chicken daily from trusted suppliers and skewers each order individually rather than in advance, grilling over Kishu binchotan charcoal to keep the meat tender while concentrating its umami, with the heat and timing carefully judged for aroma. Signature skewers include the tori-negi (chicken and scallion), prized for its overwhelming portion of meat layered with vegetables and served with a house tare refined over some 30 years; the kimo (liver), grilled to a rich, almost rare-centered texture; and the seseri (chicken neck), valued for its springy, marbled bite and finished with Miyakojima sea salt.

anecdotes.text: Kobayakawa began his career at 21 in a Western/French-style restaurant before taking over a franchise location at 27, and in 2006 opened Baji Tofu of his own, picking yakitori because it is widely and lastingly loved.

Each skewer is strung to order and grilled over binchotan charcoal to keep the meat tender and the umami concentrated; the seseri (neck) is finished with Miyakojima sea salt and the tori-negi is served with a house tare developed over roughly 30 years.
The counter room is kept dim, lit largely by the bright flames of Kishu binchotan charcoal, a quiet, grown-up space for savoring skewers one at a time.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hitosara's chef profile confirms 小早川賢治 was born in 京都 in 1960, began cooking at 21 in a Western/French kitchen, ran a franchise at 27, and opened 馬耳東風 in 2006, choosing yakitori as a widely-loved genre; it details the 鶏ねぎ (圧倒的なボリューム, 30-year 秘伝のタレ), kimo, and せせり finished with 宮古島の塩, grilled to order over 備長炭. Gnavi/search confirm the Muromachi-dori location and the dim, Kishu-binchotan-lit adult counter atmosphere. The 'suguki welcome pickle' and specific ground-floor seat count were unverifiable and removed.

Even salt-only (塩) skewers, while reducing direct gluten exposure, cannot be considered celiac-safe given the shared grill surface and the pervasive use of soy sauce and tare nearby.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Yakitori glaze (tare) and soy-based seasonings are central to the menu, and most Japanese soy sauce and tare contain wheat. Tare skewers should be treated as containing gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is a chicken-focused yakitori restaurant; there is no vegan program and even non-meat items (such as grilled vegetables) are cooked on the same charcoal grill used for chicken, so cross-contact with animal products should be assumed.

positives.text: Chicken is sourced fresh daily and skewers are prepared and grilled to order over binchotan charcoal, so guests can order item by item and ask about preparation; salt (塩) seasoning is available as an alternative to tare for those wanting to reduce soy/wheat exposure, though it is not gluten-free.

chef_bio.background: Kuchibashi Modan opened in August 2013 on Nagahara-cho in the heart of Kyoto's Shijo-Kawaramachi district, a short walk from Kawaramachi Station. The owner came up through traditional Japanese-cuisine (washoku) kitchens before striking out with this charcoal yakitori counter, and that grounding shows from the very first dish: even the otoshi (opening small plate) is made with care. The result is a stylish, almost wine-bar feel where you can settle in casually at the counter or a table and watch the skewers cook over binchotan charcoal.
chef_bio.philosophy: Hospitality-forward and detail-driven: regulars note that the owner and staff put real care into both the cooking and the welcome, and that the meticulousness of a Japanese-cuisine background carries through every plate.
chef_bio.specialty: The kitchen is built around 'hinedori' (mature laying hens) prized for their deeper flavor and firmer, more satisfying bite than young chicken. It is served as a single omakase course (around seven grilled items plus a few small plates and a finishing dish), running through cuts like seseri (neck), negima, tebakawa (wing skin) and jidori thigh. The signature is the tsukune (chicken meatball), browned and fragrant on the outside, fluffy within, rolled through a rich egg yolk and brightened with grated daikon. Raw chicken preparations, including chicken sashimi, round out the experience.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers describe a tsukune with a fragrant browned surface and fluffy center, eaten by rolling it through a rich egg yolk and refreshing grated daikon.
The owner trained in traditional Japanese cuisine, and diners note that even the opening otoshi plate is full of care; the skewers are grilled over charcoal in a stylish, bar-like room.
The course is described as a 'beautifully composed yakitori course where the flavor of hinedori (mature hen) stands out,' and the shop is a repeat Tabelog 'Yakitori WEST Top 100' selection.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, Japan (Nakagyo Ward, near Karasuma Oike Station)
chef_bio.background: Tori Saki is the Kyoto yakitori counter of chef Tomoki Hata, a Kyoto native born in 1983. Hata entered the world of yakitori at 19, and later moved to Tokyo alone to apprentice for three years under Yoshiteru Ikegawa at the Michelin-starred Meguro restaurant Tori Shiki, one of the most respected yakitori houses in Japan. He brought that technique home, opening Tori Saki in November 2019 inside a renovated Kyoto townhouse (machiya) with a counter seating about fifteen, plus a small private room, where guests watch the grilling up close. The room is intimate and reservation-only, and the cooking centers on a single hearth of Kishu binchotan charcoal.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on fire: maximizing each ingredient through strong, close-flame grilling and careful, skewer-by-skewer heat control, in the tradition Hata trained in.
chef_bio.specialty: Chicken, cooked over fierce, close binchotan heat in the high-flame style Hata learned at Tori Shiki, which sears the surface fast while keeping the inside juicy. The omakase walks through the bird cut by cut, finished in salt or tare depending on the piece, with skewers such as kashiwa (thigh), seseri (neck), sunagimo (gizzard), tsukune, and grilled vegetables like shiitake. The meal opens with pickles and closes with a rice bowl, with chicken soboro-don and oyakodon appearing at the finish.

anecdotes.text: Hata started in yakitori at age 19 and later apprenticed for three years under Yoshiteru Ikegawa at the Michelin-starred Tori Shiki in Meguro, Tokyo, before returning to his hometown of Kyoto to open his own counter.
Tori Saki opened in 2019 in a renovated Kyoto machiya, working from a single hearth of Kishu binchotan charcoal and the high-heat grilling method carried over from Tori Shiki.
Diners describe the kitchen's hallmark as exceptional yakitori grilled over close, strong heat, with each skewer landing at a consistent, careful level of doneness.

The shop previously built a following for its animal-free vegan ramen, then reopened in June 2023 as a reservation-only venue with a renewed vegan tsukemen.

chef_bio.background: Soshoku Cafe Ren is run by a Taiwanese woman who came to Japan at age 22 for language study and settled after marrying a Japanese husband. After recovering from a serious liver illness that required major surgery, she embraced vegetarianism and Taiwanese Buddhist 'su si' cooking, eventually opening Ren to share that cuisine. The brand has grown to three locations across Kyoto plus one in Wakayama, with this Shijo-Omiya branch set in a renovated machiya townhouse on a quiet residential lane.
chef_bio.philosophy: A strict no-animal-products ethos (no meat, fish, eggs or dairy) rooted in Buddhist vegetarian practice, also excluding the five pungent vegetables, paired with a wish to share the wonder of vegetarian food with everyone from children to the elderly, and a stated commitment to animal welfare and the environment. Vegetables are grown without pesticides or chemical fertilizers in Wakayama and Kyoto.
chef_bio.specialty: Taiwanese Buddhist-style vegetarian cuisine: a daily set meal with two mains, five sides, brown rice (mixed with black rice) and an herbal medicinal soup simmered from more than 15 Chinese herbs for about two hours; yakuzen (medicinal) curry; and playful mock dishes such as 'vegan eel,' fried soy-meat with mugwort and lotus root, and pumpkin tempura.

It occupies a converted Japanese townhouse that previously served as a glassworks and a dango (rice-dumpling) shop, now given a warm, retro feel. chef_bio.philosophy: The owners describe their approach as 'treat each day with care,' favoring a simple 'one vegetable, one dish' honesty over elaborate technique, and cooking with organic produce sourced from nearby Uji-area farmers.

places.vegan_detail: Shourin-ji is a Rinzai Zen temple (a sub-temple of Tofukuji). Two food offerings exist: (1) matcha green tea served with Japanese sweets after a zazen/sutra-copying session (a choice of dry sweets / higashi for about 800 yen or fresh sweets / namagashi for about 1000 yen added to the experience), and (2) a full shojin ryori meal experience available by advance reservation (must book by 16:00 two days before). Because it is a temple kitchen, the meal itself is reliably vegan; the accompanying wagashi sweets are traditionally vegan but the exact sweets vary, so confirm ingredients of the specific sweet on the day. No menu page independently itemizes every ingredient, so vegans should still state their requirement when booking.

chef_bio.background: Shourin-ji (毘沙門堂 勝林寺) is a Rinzai Zen sub-temple (tatchu) of the great Tofukuji temple complex in Kyoto's Higashiyama district, founded in 1550. Its principal deity is Bishamonten, a guardian of fortune and victory, and the temple historically protected the northern direction of Tofukuji. In recent years it has become well known to visitors for its seasonal flower-water basins (hanachozu), goshuin calligraphy, and hands-on Zen experiences.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rooted in Zen Buddhist practice, the temple frames eating, meditation and copying scriptures as a single mindful experience open even to first-time and solo visitors.
chef_bio.specialty: Zazen (seated meditation) and sutra/Buddha-image copying sessions, finished with matcha and Japanese sweets; a full shojin ryori (Buddhist vegetarian) meal is available by advance reservation. The plant-based meal follows Zen kitchen tradition, using kelp- and shiitake-based dashi instead of any animal stock.

anecdotes.text: The temple is widely featured for its photogenic seasonal hanachozu (flower-filled water basins) and goshuin, alongside zazen, sutra-copying and Buddha-image copying experiences that beginners and solo visitors can join by reservation.

After a meditation or copying session, visitors are served matcha with a choice of dry sweets (about 800 yen) or fresh sweets (about 1000 yen); a separate shojin ryori meal (from about 3,630 yen) can be reserved up to 16:00 two days in advance.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: souda-kyoto / ja.kyoto.travel: 勝林寺 founded 1550, a normally-closed tatchu of Tofukuji enshrining Bishamonten and protecting the northern direction; zazen (adult 1,500 yen) plus sutra/Buddha-image copying, hanachozu and goshuin. shourin-ji.org: matcha with dry sweets 800 yen or fresh sweets 1,000 yen; shojin ryori from 3,630 yen reservable by 16:00 two days in advance.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free handling information is published. Shojin ryori and accompanying wagashi commonly include wheat (soy sauce, fu/wheat gluten, batter, sweets), so cross-contamination cannot be ruled out and must be discussed when reserving.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No statement that wheat-free tamari is used. Shojin cooking typically uses standard wheat-containing soy sauce unless specially arranged, so assume soy sauce contains wheat unless confirmed otherwise.

vegan_cross_contact.text: As a Zen temple kitchen serving only shojin ryori, no meat, fish, eggs or dairy are used on site, which greatly reduces animal cross-contact compared with an omnivore restaurant.

staff_allergy_handling.text: VegeMap notes that visitors should inform staff of dietary requirements and allergies before ordering; the temple takes reservations by phone (075-561-4311) and web form, which is the channel to arrange a vegan and/or allergy-aware meal.

positives.text: Listed as fully vegan (all-vegan) on Japan VegeMap, consistent with the temple's shojin ryori tradition that excludes all animal products and uses kelp/shiitake dashi rather than fish stock.
Plant-based meals and matcha-with-sweets are prepared in a temple kitchen with no animal-protein cooking, so the risk of meat or fish cross-contact is inherently low.

cultural_comfort.note: A foreign student is welcome but should expect a Japanese-language temple setting; reservations are made through the website form, and basic Japanese or a translation app helps, especially for arranging a vegan shojin ryori meal.

chef_bio.background: Natural Food Village was opened in 2001 by Tatsu, a musician who spent about four years backpacking around Japan and the world before settling in the Ichijoji neighborhood of Kyoto. It is widely cited as one of the oldest fully vegan restaurants in the city, founded back when 'vegan' and 'organic' were still unfamiliar words in Japan. Tatsu describes the restaurant's aesthetic as 'stateless' rather than multicultural, blending the many cultures he encountered while traveling.
chef_bio.philosophy: Tatsu's guiding idea is that 'food creates the body, and music and art create the heart and spirit' — he sees good health as the foundation for truly enjoying music and life. The kitchen prioritizes organic, pesticide-free vegetables, carefully chosen safe seasonings, and groundwater sourced from Kitashirakawa.
chef_bio.specialty: International creative vegan cuisine; the signature Rainbow Bento (虹色御膳) with seven deli-style sides, ancient grains and soup, plus soy-cutlet rice bowls, Thai-style fried noodles, tempeh tempura, spring rolls and curry.

anecdotes.text: The space doubles as a live-music venue; weekend nights often feature local musicians performing or jamming, reflecting Tatsu's background as a musician.
Tatsu travels personally to draw groundwater from Kitashirakawa for the restaurant, and some longtime regulars have been inspired by the food ethos to take up farming themselves.

chef_bio.background: Izusen has served Kyoto's Buddhist vegetarian (shojin) cuisine since 1963 from a tranquil sub-temple, Daiji-in, within the grounds of Daitoku-ji — one of the head temples of Rinzai Zen. Guests dine looking out over a temple garden, eating from tetsubachi: round iron bowls that, in the Buddhist tradition, monks once carried to receive alms of food.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen follows the Zen ideal of three hearts: kishin (a joyful heart in cooking), roshin (a respectful heart that wastes nothing, attending to each grain of rice), and daishin (a compassionate, magnanimous heart). Meat, fish and seafood are excluded entirely, seasonings are kept restrained to let natural flavors speak, and every part of an ingredient is used.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature is shojin tetsubachi-ryori — seasonal vegetable, grain and legume dishes presented in nested iron-bowl vessels, offered as fixed seasonal courses (Ayame, Yuri, Botan). Tea-kaiseki (chakaiseki) is also served.

anecdotes.text: The tetsubachi (iron bowl) at the heart of the meal traces back to the alms bowls of Buddhist monks, an implement said to have come from India and reached Japan in the Nara period — here repurposed as elegant tableware merging Zen with Kyoto cuisine.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official Izusen site confirms the 1963 Daiji-in shojin restaurant within Daitoku-ji, the tetsubachi iron-bowl format (traced to Indian alms bowls that reached Japan in the Nara period), the three hearts (kishin/roshin/daishin) and the Ayame/Yuri/Botan seasonal courses.

chef_bio.background: Kyono Juice opened in 2018 as the antenna shop of Chlorelland Corp., a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Kyoto health-food company Sun Chlorella. It sits on the busy northwest corner of the Shimogamo Honmachi and Kitaoji intersection in a striking modern storefront, with a second-floor seating area for lingering over a drink.
chef_bio.philosophy: The team set out to bring cold-pressed juice culture — popular among health- and beauty-conscious people and vegetarians in the US — to Japan, spreading it 'from Kyoto's Shimogamo,' with a focus on drinks that are gentle on the body and deliver fruit-and-vegetable nutrition in an easily absorbed form. anecdotes.text: Billed in local food press as one of Kyoto's first cold-pressed juice shops, it pitched the then-novel idea of nutrient-dense raw juice with live enzymes and only the soluble fiber, marketed for quick absorption and lighter digestion.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood juice stand where pointing at the menu and a friendly konnichiwa go a long way; staff are unlikely to conduct detailed allergen conversations in English, so know your key Japanese food words.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official Izusen site confirms the Murasakino branch at Daitoku-ji's gate since 1977, the sister Daiji-in branch since 1963, the teppachi iron-bowl shojin format and the yuba-kaiseki, Unsui and Ayame courses (grains/legumes/vegetables only, no meat or seafood).

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional temple-gate shojin restaurant popular with international visitors; staff are used to foreign diners and English menus/listings exist, but a few words of Japanese and politeness go a long way in this formal Zen setting.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, Japan (Obaku Zen Buddhist temple, founded 1671)
chef_bio.background: Kanga-an is a Zen temple of the Obaku (Obakushu) school, full name 黄檗禅宗 瑞芝山 閑臥庵, founded in 1671. It was established when the guardian deity Chintaku Reifujin was brought from Kifune (Kibune) Shrine to protect the imperial capital, and the temple is tied to Emperor Go-Mizunoo, who favored it as a peaceful retreat. For more than 300 years it has carried on the fucha ryori tradition of the Obaku monks.
chef_bio.philosophy: Fucha means 'serving tea widely to many people,' and the cuisine embodies communal, egalitarian dining — dishes are traditionally shared among diners seated together, with no one superior or inferior. Unlike austere temple fare, Kanga-an's fucha is colorful and celebratory, while remaining rooted in Zen vegetarian principles and the Obaku monks' reputation for healthful longevity through this oil-rich plant-based diet.
chef_bio.specialty: Fucha ryori (普茶料理) — the Obaku school's distinctive plant-based Buddhist banquet cuisine, served as multi-course set meals (Murasaki-zen, Take-zen, Shu-zen, Kuro-zen). Signature dishes include a remarkable plant-based 'vegan eel' crafted from tofu, seaweed and burdock, deep-fried preparations, and colorful kaiseki-style presentations.

anecdotes.text: The Obaku monks who ate fucha cuisine continuously were known for their longevity, attributed to the healthy plant-based, oil-conscious cooking.
Within the temple grounds is a hidden bar overlooking the Japanese garden, where guests can relax with a drink after the course meal.
A signature dish is a plant-based 'unagi (eel)' made from tofu, seaweed and burdock, showcasing the inventive imitation dishes central to fucha ryori.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kangaan.jp and visitjapan-vegetarian confirm the 1671 Obaku Zen temple, its tie to Emperor Go-Mizunoo and the Kibune guardian deity Chintaku Reifujin, the shared/egalitarian fucha ryori, the tofu-seaweed-burdock 'vegan eel' and the garden bar.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Fucha ryori is defined by its skillful use of oil and includes deep-fried dishes (tempura, fried imitation items); these batters are typically wheat-based, so gluten cross-contact in fryers is likely. Not confirmed whether any GF accommodation exists.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a traditional Japanese temple kitchen, the cuisine uses standard soy sauce and sweet glazes, which normally contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is advertised. Assume soy seasonings contain gluten unless confirmed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is a Buddhist (shojin/fucha) kitchen serving no meat, fish or animal products, so animal cross-contact is inherently minimal — a strong positive for vegans and vegetarians.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Meals are completely reservation-only and arranged 2-3 days in advance, which gives the kitchen the opportunity to note dietary needs; however, no published allergen protocol was found, so specific allergies should be raised directly when booking.

positives.text: Entirely plant-based Buddhist temple cuisine — no meat or fish in the kitchen — making it one of the safest choices in Kyoto for vegans and vegetarians.
Shojin/fucha tradition uses kombu and shiitake dashi rather than fish-based dashi, so the umami base is plant-derived.
positives.why: The cited page contains no mention of dashi, kombu or shiitake anywhere; it only says 精進料理, which by definition excludes fish dashi. Rewrite to what the page supports or drop it — as written it is generic tradition asserted as a venue fact.

cultural_comfort.note: It is a traditional temple kaiseki experience that is completely reservation-only and best arranged in advance (often via an English booking concierge), so a few words of Japanese or an interpreter-style booking service smooths the visit.

It serves a fully plant-based, multinational take on Kyoto cooking — a modern, westernized cousin of shojin ryori — built around seasonal Kyoto vegetables together with fresh yuba (tofu skin) and namafu (fresh wheat gluten).
chef_bio.philosophy: A quality-over-volume ethos: the kitchen deliberately limits how many guests it takes so each course can be prepared with care and presented as 'a work of art.' Everything is 100% plant-based — no dairy, eggs, fish, meat or honey — using Kyoto's seasonal produce.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers repeatedly single out the faux-sushi plate, which convincingly replicates eel, tuna and scallops, and a remarkably creamy matcha tofu cheesecake, describing the cooking as creative and meticulously presented.

The owner reportedly has food allergies themselves and understands the challenges, occasionally making accommodations when no other guests are present, though they state they normally do not handle allergy requests.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, Japan — Saga-Arashiyama, on the grounds of Tenryu-ji temple.
chef_bio.background: Shigetsu is the dining hall of Tenryu-ji, the head temple of the Tenryu-ji branch of Rinzai Zen Buddhism and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Arashiyama. The restaurant occupies the Ryumontei pavilion within the temple's celebrated Sogen Pond garden and is run directly by the temple, serving the shojin ryori that grew out of Zen monastic practice.
chef_bio.philosophy: Shojin ryori embodies the Buddhist principle of reverence for life: meals are made entirely from plants — no meat, fish, or animal products — and traditionally without the five pungent vegetables, harmonizing with nature and the seasons. Diners are invited to eat mindfully, reflecting the Zen view of eating as part of spiritual training.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal shojin ryori multi-dish set meals (Yuki, Tsuki, Hana) centered on goma-dofu (sesame tofu), yuba, miso-glazed and simmered seasonal vegetables, mountain vegetables, and pickles, served in private tatami rooms overlooking the garden.

anecdotes.text: Recognized in the MICHELIN Guide Kyoto-Osaka as a Bib Gourmand (exceptional food at moderate prices) and awarded a MICHELIN Green Star for its sustainable, plant-based ethos.

A vegan diner described being 'stunned before we even tasted one bite of food,' served roughly 11–12 artfully arranged dishes — chilled sesame tofu, yuba in clear broth, miso-glazed eggplant — while dining shoeless in a private tatami room with shoji doors opening onto the Tenryu-ji gardens.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tenryu-ji's official pages and Kyoto tourism listings confirm Shigetsu is temple-run, served in the Ryumontei hall beside the Sogenchi pond garden, offering the Yuki/Tsuki/Hana shojin sets, and note its Michelin Bib Gourmand + Green Star listing.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No source documents a gluten-free protocol or how shared cookware is handled. As traditional shojin-ryori, dishes are generally light and plant-based, but gluten-containing items are common in this style of cooking — wheat-gluten products such as fu (wheat gluten / nama-fu) and seitan-like ingredients are staples of Buddhist temple cuisine, so individual dishes may contain wheat. Celiac diners should not assume the meal is gluten-free and must confirm dish by dish with staff.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce and miso glazes used in shojin ryori typically contain wheat; the restaurant does not advertise wheat-free seasonings, so strict-GF diners should confirm in advance. (General shojin/Japanese cuisine norm; not specifically stated by the venue.)
soy_sauce_wheat.why: Page carries nothing about soy sauce, miso or allergens; the claim itself admits it is a general inference, so the source should be nulled / flagged as inference rather than pointing at the venue page.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is fully plant-based — no animal-based ingredients are used at all ('動物性の素材を一切使用せず') — so there is no meat or fish cross-contact in the kitchen.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Meals are reservation-based by phone (075-882-9725, 9:00–17:00), giving an opportunity to communicate allergies or dietary needs ahead of the visit; no formal allergy-handling program is published.

positives.text: Entirely vegan kitchen: a temple-run shojin ryori operation that uses zero animal products, with plant-based (kombu/seaweed) dashi rather than fish dashi — eliminating dairy, egg, meat and fish cross-contact concerns.
positives.why: The kombu/seaweed-dashi detail is not on this page at all; the vegan substance is better sourced to the venue's own 動物性の素材を一切使用せず sentence. Repoint to https://www.tenryuji.com/shigetsu/ and drop the dashi specific unless separately evidenced.

positives.text: Set-course format with consistent, well-documented dishes (sesame tofu, yuba, simmered seasonal vegetables) makes it easy to know what you are eating.

cultural_comfort.note: A famous tourist temple that welcomes many foreign visitors and has an English website, but the dining service itself is traditional and Japanese-run, so a few polite Japanese phrases (and a phone reservation, ideally with help) smooth the experience.

places.name: 白雲庵 (Hakuunan)
places.gf_detail: Not gluten-free by default. Fucha ryori centers on wheat-heavy preparations: seasoned tempura (wheat-flour battered and fried), mock-meat "modoki" dishes that often use wheat gluten (fu/seitan), and Japanese soy sauce that typically contains wheat. There is no published gluten-free menu and no information about a dedicated fryer. A celiac/gluten-sensitive diner would need to discuss this directly when reserving (reservation required by 5pm the previous day), and even then safe options would likely be very limited. places.vegan_detail: Hakuunan serves traditional Obaku fucha ryori (普茶料理), a Chinese-derived form of Buddhist shojin cuisine that is plant-based by tradition: no meat, fish, eggs or dairy. The standard course is built on "two soups and six dishes" (二汁六菜) and includes sesame tofu (goma-dofu), yoshino-ni stew, seasonal vegetables and seasoned tempura. Classic shojin/fucha cooking generally avoids animal products, but some traditional kitchens use bonito (katsuo) dashi unless kombu-only stock is requested, so vegans should state their needs when reserving. The restaurant's listing advises telling staff about vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies so the menu can be adjusted, and both vegan and vegetarian course options are noted as available. Treat it as plant-based-by-default but confirm dashi and any honey at booking.

chef_bio.background: Hakuunan is a long-established fucha ryori restaurant set directly across from the main gate of Obaku-san Manpuku-ji, the head temple of the Obaku Zen school in Uji — an area famous as a birthplace of Uji tea. The Obaku school was founded in Japan by the Chinese monk Ingen (Yinyuan Longqi), who arrived in 1654 and brought with him 'fucha ryori,' a Chinese-style Buddhist vegetarian cuisine distinct from native Japanese shojin ryori.
chef_bio.philosophy: Faithful to the Obaku fucha tradition introduced from Ming-dynasty China, the kitchen turns carefully selected seasonal vegetables and plant proteins into refined, colorful dishes — vegetarian cooking treated as a guest-honoring art rather than austere abstinence.
chef_bio.specialty: Obaku fucha ryori served as a 'two soups and six dishes' course: sesame tofu (goma-dofu), yoshino-ni stew, seasonal vegetable preparations and seasoned tempura, plated to be visually elegant and rich in flavor despite being entirely plant-based.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant sits at the gate of Manpuku-ji, founded by the Chinese monk Ingen, who introduced fucha ryori to Japan in the 17th century — making Hakuunan a place to taste one of Japan's four great schools of Buddhist vegetarian cuisine in its home setting.
Its signature course follows the classic '二汁六菜' (two soups, six dishes) format, featuring goma-dofu (sesame tofu) and seasoned tempura among the carefully selected seasonal dishes.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official hakuunan.com describes it as a fucha ryori (精進料理) 老舗 at Manpuku-ji's gate serving a 二汁六菜 course of goma-dofu, yoshino-ni and 味付天麩羅, and notes it accommodates even single diners.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Fucha courses include seasoned tempura, deep-fried in wheat-flour batter; no dedicated gluten-free fryer is documented, so shared frying oil is likely.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No wheat-free soy sauce (tamari) is advertised; standard Japanese shoyu used in shojin/fucha cooking typically contains wheat. Confirm at booking if gluten is a concern.

vegan_cross_contact.text: As a dedicated Buddhist fucha/shojin kitchen, the menu is plant-based by tradition with no meat, fish, eggs or dairy prepared on site, greatly reducing animal cross-contact.
Some traditional shojin kitchens use bonito-based dashi unless kombu-only stock is requested; vegans should confirm the dashi when reserving.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The restaurant's listing advises diners to tell staff about vegetarian/vegan requirements and any allergies so the menu can be chosen accordingly, indicating willingness to accommodate stated needs.

positives.text: Fully plant-based Buddhist temple cuisine: no meat, fish, shellfish, dairy, eggs or honey by tradition, so no risk of animal-protein contamination from a mixed menu.
Reservation-only (by 5pm the prior day) means the kitchen can prepare for your dietary needs in advance rather than improvising on the spot.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a traditional, reservation-only temple-cuisine restaurant where some basic Japanese and advance booking (by phone or online the day before) will smooth things, though a polite konnichiwa and clearly stated dietary needs go a long way.

places.name: 東林院 (Tōrin-in)
places.gf_detail: No gluten-free information is published. Shojin ryori relies heavily on regular Japanese soy sauce (which normally contains wheat) for simmered dishes and dressings, and may include wheat gluten preparations (fu) and tofu products marinated in soy sauce. There is no indication of wheat-free soy sauce or a dedicated GF kitchen. A gluten-sensitive or celiac diner must inquire directly in advance; assume soy sauce contains wheat unless confirmed otherwise.
places.vegan_detail: Tōrin-in serves traditional shojin ryori (Buddhist temple cuisine), which by religious practice excludes all meat, fish, and animal products — it is plant-based throughout. The abbot Nishikawa Genbō, a published shojin cookbook author, prepares the meals. Documented dishes include rice, mushroom-and-mitsuba clear soup, chrysanthemum-greens shiraae (tofu dressing), simmered carrot and burdock, furofuki daikon, and pickles; seasonal events such as the Azuki-gayu (red-bean rice porridge) gathering serve azuki porridge, simmered black beans, daikon with abura-age, rape-blossom shiraae, and salted kelp. Shojin ryori traditionally uses kombu (kelp) and shiitake dashi rather than fish (bonito) dashi, so the broth is plant-based — but specific ingredient confirmation is not published, so a strict vegan should still confirm on the day.
places.hours_raw: Regular shojin ryori lunch is by reservation; weekly cooking classes Tue & Fri 10:00-13:00. Special seasonal openings (no reservation): "Admiring the Sal Blossoms" gathering mid-June to early July and "Azuki-gayu" gathering in mid-to-late January, roughly 9:30-15:00 (last entry 14:30), serving shojin meals. The temple is otherwise normally closed to the general public.

chef_bio.origin: Hanazono, Kyoto — within the Myoshin-ji temple grounds
chef_bio.background: Tōrin-in is a sub-temple of the great Rinzai Zen complex of Myoshin-ji, founded in 1531 by Hosokawa Ujitsuna to honor his late father and later rebuilt by the warlord Yamana Toyokuni. Its main image is Kannon Bosatsu. The temple is famous as the 'temple of the sal trees' (sarasōju), with more than a dozen Japanese stewartia in the front garden whose white blossoms fall in a single day during the rainy season — the source of its celebrated June-July 'Admiring the Sal Blossoms' gathering.
chef_bio.philosophy: The abbot teaches not just cooking but the spirit of shojin — wasting no ingredient and minimizing waste of water and electricity — treating the meal as Zen practice. Guests describe gentle, refined, distinctly Kyoto flavors.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal shojin ryori (Zen vegetarian temple cuisine): rice, clear soups, tofu shiraae dressings, simmered vegetables, furofuki daikon, and the wintertime azuki red-bean porridge served at the New Year Azuki-gayu gathering.

anecdotes.text: The resident abbot Nishikawa Genbō entered Zen training at Ryoan-ji and Zuiryu-ji and became head priest of Tōrin-in in 1984; he opened the normally-closed temple to the public, offering shojin meals, temple lodging, and weekly cooking classes, and has authored several shojin cookbooks including works on Zen temple home cooking.
Every Tuesday and Friday the abbot personally teaches a shojin ryori class in the temple's training hall, sharing both recipes and the mindful, anti-waste ethos behind them.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyounoryouri.jp confirms Nishikawa Genbō is abbot of Tōrin-in at Myoshin-ji, trained at Ryoan-ji and Zuiryu-ji, became head priest in 1984 and is a published shojin author; kyoto-kankou lists his Tuesday/Friday shojin-ryori training classes; shukuken confirms the sal-tree and Azuki-gayu events.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No information is published on whether the soy sauce, dressings, or simmering liquids are wheat-free; standard Japanese soy sauce used in temple cooking normally contains wheat, so gluten-sensitive diners should assume wheat is present unless confirmed.

positives.text: This is a fully plant-based shojin ryori kitchen run by a Zen temple, so by religious practice no meat or fish is used — there is no animal cross-contact in the cooking, a strong baseline for vegan diners.
Meals are prepared by the abbot himself, a published shojin cookbook author, with documented all-vegetable menus (e.g., shiraae tofu dressings, simmered vegetables, furofuki daikon, azuki porridge).

cultural_comfort.note: This is a working Zen sub-temple run by a Japanese-speaking abbot with a formal reservation-by-postcard system and no published English support, so a foreign student should arrange a Japanese-speaking helper and basic temple etiquette in advance.

chef_bio.background: apelila is a 100% plant-based bakery and café tucked into the Takano neighborhood of Sakyo Ward, a short walk from Demachiyanagi station and Shimogamo Shrine, sitting along the river on Kawabata-dori. It was opened in 2015 by owner-baker Takahashi Sayaka, who had previously taught bread-making classes before turning her craft into a shop offering more than 20 kinds of bread.
chef_bio.philosophy: Takahashi-san is reportedly not vegan herself; she chooses to bake entirely without animal-derived ingredients because she wants people to discover how delicious naturally-fermented yeast and simple, well-sourced ingredients can be. The shop leans on sustainability and quality: in-house milled Kyoto-grown whole wheat, organic dried fruit, and a decades-old starter.
chef_bio.specialty: Naturally-leavened vegan breads and baked goods made with a house-milled Kyoto whole-wheat flour and a sourdough starter that has been continuously fed for roughly two decades; plus a café lunch headlined by a vegan cheeseburger plate with a chickpea patty and fermented soy yogurt, alongside donuts, melon bread, caramel cream pastries, cookies and waffles.

anecdotes.text: The bread is built on a natural sourdough starter that has been continuously fed and kept alive for roughly 19–20 years, paired with whole-wheat flour milled in-house from Kyoto-grown grain.
Takahashi Sayaka opened apelila in 2015 after previously running bread-making classes, and keeps animal ingredients out of her bread to let customers taste the umami of fermentation.
The café has a calming atmosphere with a small zen garden and a back seating area where diners remove their shoes.

chef_bio.background: Hobodo is a tiny vegan cafe-and-bookshop run by a husband-and-wife team, Daijiro and Misayo Satoh, who opened it in 2014. Daijiro handles the coffee (using beans from a local Kyoto roaster, Cafe de Corazon, with an Italian Blend and Panama variety), while Misayo, who lives a plant-based lifestyle, cooks the food. The couple deliberately keep the place small, book-filled and open only a few days a week so guests can linger and read while they eat.
chef_bio.philosophy: They named the cafe after early-20th-century American 'hobos,' embracing a free, independent spirit. The kitchen is entirely plant-based so that, in their words, everyone can sit down and eat together without worry; they prioritize seasonal vegetables from local organic and natural farms and balance the shop around family life.
chef_bio.specialty: A daily-changing vegetable set meal (brown or edamame rice, miso soup and several seasonal vegetable side dishes), plus several kinds of brown-rice ohagi in unusual flavors (egoma/perilla, rum-raisin, hazelnut, roasted-tea and more), spring rolls, falafel and homemade flatbread.

anecdotes.text: The couple chose the name 'Hobodo' in homage to American hobos of the early 1900s, embracing that wandering, independent spirit for their homey DIY cafe.
Misayo creates a fully vegan menu specifically so that 'everyone can eat together without concern,' sourcing produce directly from organic and naturally-cultivated farms.

Their weekly-changing brown-rice-and-seasonal-vegetable bento is popular as a takeaway to carry to the rooftop terrace of the Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art (the 'Higashiyama Cube'), a short walk away.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: karafuneya and other Kyoto listings say the Satoh couple opened Hobodo in 2014, open only a few days a week; Daijiro sources beans from roaster Cafe de Corazon; the name honors early-1900s American hobos; crea.bunshun recommends buying its brown-rice/vegetable bento to eat at the nearby Kyocera Museum rooftop terrace.

chef_bio.background: KAMOGAWA BAKERY opened on October 31, 2020 in Kyoto's Kamigyo Ward, just west of the Kamogawa River near the Imperial Palace. It was created so that vegetarians, vegans and people with egg or dairy allergies could enjoy genuinely delicious bread alongside everyone else, baking with 100% Japanese wheat and plant-derived ingredients instead of the butter and milk usually relied on in baking.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's theme is 'ONE TABLE' - the idea that bread lovers and allergy sufferers can all sit at the same table and enjoy the same bread. Around 80% of the lineup is plant-based, and the bakery also pursues sustainability, using compostable cups for takeaway drinks, ethically sourced coffee, and supporting food-donation and children's-meal programs.
chef_bio.specialty: Chewy bagels made with Hokkaido 'Yumechikara' wheat, a soy-milk-butter 'new white bread'/shokupan made with Hokkaido 'Haruyokoi' wheat, and bagel sandwiches including a Kyoto shibazuke-pickle bagel using pickles from the established Kawakatsu Sohonke.

anecdotes.text: The bakery substitutes soy-milk butter for dairy so its signature 'new white bread' tastes sweet and creamy with no milk or butter, and it uses plant-based ingredients across roughly 80% of its lineup.
There is a second-floor cafe space where customers can sit and eat in, and an egg-allergy-friendly 'hobo-tama' (almost-egg) sandwich on the menu.

chef_bio.background: Pettirosso is a tiny owner-run plant-based restaurant created by chef Ayako Hayashi and her Italian husband, Marco. Ayako met Marco while studying to become a chef in Italy, and the two run the place themselves. After working in vegan cooking and operating a restaurant in the Shijo Tominokoji area of central Kyoto for about five years, they relocated in May 2023 to a quiet residential pocket of Kita-ku, just a few minutes' walk from the Kamo River, and made the kitchen fully vegan.
chef_bio.philosophy: A deep appreciation for local, seasonal Kyoto vegetables expressed through an Italian-Japanese fusion: nuts add richness, fermented foods deepen flavor, and spices act as accents. The couple chose the new location to feel nature nearby, encouraging guests to take a vegan lunch box to enjoy along the Kamo River. The menu rotates roughly every two weeks to follow what is in season.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal one-plate vegan lunches and multi-course vegan dinners built from more than 30 kinds of organic Kyoto vegetables (from Ohara, Hanase and nearby areas). Signature dishes include a vegan broccoli-and-almond lasagna and a vegan carrot cake; egg-, dairy- and refined-sugar-free vegan sweets are a highlight.

anecdotes.text: Chef Ayako Hayashi met her Italian husband Marco while studying culinary arts in Italy; the couple now runs the entire restaurant by themselves.
They relocated in May 2023 to be near nature, and recommend taking a vegan lunch box just a few minutes' walk to the Kamo River.
The kitchen uses over 30 kinds of organic Kyoto vegetables, with a menu that changes about every two weeks to follow the season.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Leaf Kyoto and DigiStyle Kyoto confirm chef Ayako Hayashi and Italian husband Marco, the ~5-year Shijo Tominokoji predecessor, the May 24 2023 relocation to Izumoji Tatehoncho in Kita-ku near the Kamo River, the fully vegan turn, 30+ organic Kyoto vegetables, biweekly seasonal menu, and the almond lasagna and carrot cake.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is entirely plant-based with no animal products used, which greatly reduces the risk of meat, fish or dairy cross-contact.

chef_bio.background: OyOy opened in June 2020 on the first floor of the Shinpuhkan complex by Karasuma Oike Station as a hybrid bookshop, cafe and vegetable shop. It is a collaboration between Saka no Tochu (坂ノ途中), a Kyoto organic-vegetable company that sources seasonal produce grown without pesticides or chemical fertilizers from partner farms, and Oraido (鴎来堂), the team behind Kamome Books in Kagurazaka, Tokyo, who curate the in-store library.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name OyOy (oioi) evokes an unhurried pace - gradually and gently bringing vegetables and books into everyday life. The shop treats vegetables as living things, each with its own flavor, form and daily change, and pairs them with a curated shelf of books on food, farming and travel to enrich daily life.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature OyOy Seasonal Vegetable Plate, built entirely from plant-based seasonal vegetables and changing with what the farms harvest, alongside homemade desserts like seasonal tofu douhua and carrot cake, in-house fruit cordials, and Umi no Mukou coffee from Saka no Tochu's coffee division.

anecdotes.text: Half the shop is lined with curated bookshelves spanning food, agriculture, daily life and travel essays, so diners can browse books and buy organically grown vegetables alongside their meal.
The full plant-based vegetable plate is offered Friday through Monday (lunch only on Monday), with the philosophy that each seasonal vegetable's individual character should be showcased.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: On-the-slope (Saka no Tochu's own project page) and vegewel confirm the June 2020 Shinpuhkan first-floor opening, the Saka no Tochu x Oraido (Kamome Books) collaboration, the plant-based seasonal vegetable plate served Friday-Monday, tofu douhua and carrot cake desserts, and Umi no Mukou coffee.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire kitchen is vegetarian with no meat or fish, so there is no animal-protein cross-contact from meat or seafood; the main risk for vegans is dairy and egg used in some desserts and light items, not shared cooking surfaces with meat.

positives.text: Fully vegetarian kitchen using organic, pesticide-free seasonal vegetables from partner farms, with a clearly designated all-plant-based vegetable plate for vegans.
Reviewers praise the vegan platter's many distinct vegetable preparations as a highlight, in a calm bookstore setting with soft jazz.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, tourist-accustomed book-cafe in a central shopping complex where a little Japanese helps, but the plant-based plate and menu are easy to navigate and staff are welcoming to foreign visitors.

chef_bio.background: Social Kitchen opened in September 2010 in a building just outside the south gate of Shokoku-ji temple in Kamigyo-ku, Kyoto. It was created by the Kyoto collective Hanare, which had been running a weekly community café since 2006. Conceived as a '21st-century community center,' the three-floor space pairs a ground-floor café and bookstore (Not Pillar Books) with a second-floor event hall for lectures, discussions, workshops and exhibitions, and a third-floor shared office for designers, programmers and art groups.
chef_bio.philosophy: The café is framed as 'a project exploring the possibilities that expand from food.' It emphasizes locally grown ingredients and a deliberately low-waste system, treating eating as part of a broader practice of community, sustainability and dialogue rather than just a meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Daily-changing lunch plates, soups, curries (including plant-based dishes such as a South Indian bean curry), plus cakes, cookies and drinks served in a relaxed café-and-bookstore setting.

anecdotes.text: The space is run by the Kyoto collective Hanare, which describes itself as pursuing practical, exciting approaches to all aspects of life — food, art, politics, economics and architecture — and had operated a weekly community café since 2006 before opening Social Kitchen in 2010.
Today the café functions as a 'share café,' with multiple cooks and small operators each taking different days of the week, so the menu and atmosphere change depending on who is in the kitchen.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Shift.jp.org confirms the September 2010 opening near Shokoku-ji in Kamigyo-ku, the Hanare collective (weekly community cafe since 2006), the three-floor layout with the ground-floor cafe and Not Pillar Books, second-floor event hall and third-floor shared office, and the locally-sourced, low-waste ethos.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is not fully vegan and rotates among different operators by day, so animal ingredients may be used on the same equipment depending on who is cooking; confirm with the day's operator.

positives.text: Plant-based dishes (such as a vegan South Indian bean curry) have been part of the café's offering, and the venue's ethos centers on local ingredients and low-waste cooking.

cultural_comfort.note: An open, internationally-minded community space used to hosting events and foreign visitors, so a friendly greeting and simple English will usually get you by, though the rotating operators may not all be fluent.

chef_bio.specialty: Kyoto-style curry udon: chewy udon in a deeply flavored ankake (thick) curry broth. The signature 'fox' (kitsune) curry udon is a house favorite; for plant-based diners they offer a vegetarian/vegan curry udon, a vegetarian ramen, and curry rice topped with vegetable tempura.

anecdotes.text: The curry udon was chosen for Japan's Cool Japan 'The Wonder 500' in 2015 as a distinctive regional product.

chef_bio.background: Browny Bread & Bagels is a well-loved Kyoto bagel specialist that began on Kitaoji-dori in the north of the city before relocating in 2016 to its current spot in the Shogoin neighborhood of Sakyo-ku, a short walk south of the Higashioji and Marutamachi intersection near Heian Shrine and Kyoto Zoo.
chef_bio.philosophy: The bakers emphasize carefully selected ingredients and extended, long-time fermentation to bring out the dough's fragrance, flavor and texture rather than relying on heavy fillings, with everything baked fresh on site each day.
chef_bio.specialty: Bagels above all: the shop keeps 20-30 varieties in stock at any time, made from domestic wheat with long fermentation and house-made yeast for a chewy, moist crumb and a deep wheat aroma. Signature flavors run from a popular cinnamon-apple-walnut with cream cheese to gorgonzola with honey and walnuts, kinako-mochi with red bean, sweet-potato cream cheese and bacon-cheese, alongside other savory breads. Bagels are graded by texture (firmer T-60 vs. softer T-70).

anecdotes.text: The shop consistently keeps 20-30 kinds of bagels on the shelves at once, spanning savory to dessert styles, and even labels them by texture grade (T-60 firmer, T-70 softer) so customers can pick the chew they like.
Originally on Kitaoji-dori, Browny moved to its current Shogoin location in 2016, settling into a small storefront near Heian Shrine and Kyoto Zoo.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: dmatcha confirms the 20-30 rotating bagel varieties, the T-60/T-70 firmness grades, domestic wheat with long fermentation, and flavors including gorgonzola-honey-walnut, kinako-mochi red bean, sweet-potato cream cheese and cinnamon-apple-walnut; kyotopi confirms the 2016 move from Kitaoji to Shogoin near Heian Shrine.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Dedicated wheat bakery making bagels, bread and focaccia from domestic wheat; gluten is pervasive throughout the kitchen and there are no gluten-free items, so this is unsafe for celiac diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: At least one variety is a soy-sauce mochi cheese bagel; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Many bagels and breads are made and baked alongside cheese, cream cheese, honey and dairy varieties on shared equipment, so vegan items are prepared in the same kitchen as animal-product items. Ask staff which specific bagels are egg-free and dairy-free.

positives.text: A HappyCow vegan-bakery directory entry notes a domestic-wheat bakeshop whose main products are bagels, white bread and focaccia, many of which are vegan-friendly, and that it offers soy milk for drinks.
Everything is baked fresh on site and the small storefront is known for friendly service.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood Japanese bakery with a takeaway counter; staff are described as friendly, but menus and bagel labels are mostly in Japanese, so a few basic Japanese phrases help when asking which bagels are egg- and dairy-free.

places.vegan_detail: Rice-bread bakery whose dough kneads freshly cooked Kyoto-blend rice into wheat flour. The base bread is plant-based, using soy milk and rice oil instead of eggs and dairy, and many items contain no eggs, dairy, or honey. Items with animal products are clearly labeled, so vegan diners can select safe options. Not all-vegan, as some products contain eggs, dairy, and honey.

The owners knead freshly cooked, just-polished Kyoto-blend rice into the dough with a mochi-pounding machine

chef_bio.background: Gohan Pan Kobo Tsubutsubu is tied to the rice shop Okui Riso Mai-ten (奥井理想米店), which handles its sales, and it debuted at the Kamigamo Shrine handmade market in summer 2012. The bakers knead freshly cooked, just-polished Kyoto-blend rice into the dough with a mochi-pounding machine rather than using rice flour.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name Tsubutsubu references ryuryu-shinku (粒粒辛苦), honoring the grain-by-grain effort of farmers and the value of every grain of rice; the shop emphasizes domestic rice and food self-sufficiency, using Hokkaido wheat chosen to avoid post-harvest pesticides.
chef_bio.specialty: Chewy, fluffy gohan pan (rice bread) made by mixing cooked rice with wheat flour for a naturally sweet, mochi-like texture; many varieties use soy milk and rice oil instead of eggs and dairy.

anecdotes.text: The bread is made from actual cooked rice pounded into the wheat dough, not rice flour, which gives its signature mochi-mochi texture and gentle sweetness.
The business began as a stall at the Kamigamo Shrine handmade market in summer 2012 and still appears at Kyoto handmade markets monthly.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site confirms that the bakery uses freshly cooked Kyoto-blend rice (not rice flour) pounded into the dough, Hokkaido wheat chosen to avoid post-harvest pesticides, soy milk and rice oil in place of eggs and dairy, the ryuryu-shinku name meaning, and that Okui Riso Mai-ten handles sales.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Not gluten-free: every bread is made with wheat flour (rice is kneaded in alongside the wheat), so gluten is present throughout the kitchen.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The facility also produces items containing eggs, dairy, peanuts, and honey, so there is cross-contamination risk for strictly plant-based diners.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Breads containing eggs or dairy are clearly labeled, helping customers avoid animal products and choose plant-based alternatives.

positives.text: The base bread is plant-based, using soy milk and rice oil instead of eggs and dairy; many items are free of eggs, dairy, and honey.
Listed on a vegan/ethical directory as a bakery with many egg-, dairy-, and honey-free items that welcomes plant-based customers.

cultural_comfort.note: Vegan-friendly spot; many such places in Kyoto are used to international visitors.

places.name: カフェ フロッシュ (Café Frosch)
places.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu or options are documented. The café's identity centers on house-baked bread made with whole-grain wheat flour and natural koji yeast, so wheat/gluten is pervasive in the kitchen. There is no information confirming wheat-free soy sauce or any gluten-free preparation. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner should treat this as not gluten-safe and ask directly before ordering.
places.vegan_detail: This is an omnivore café (it serves a German sausage sandwich and dishes that may contain dairy/eggs), but it offers a clear set of dedicated vegan options. Reported vegan items include a vegan aubergine (eggplant) burger set served with soup, side, salad and pickles; koji-bread plates with a vegan soup option; an onigiri rice-ball vegan set; and a "little bread" set with vegan soup and salad. The house bread is risen German-sourdough style using koji (a plant-based fermentation culture), and is described as entirely plant-based. Some vegetarian dishes contain dairy or eggs but can often be modified by removing animal products. Staff explicitly recommend telling them your vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies so they can guide your order.
places.hours_raw: 11:00–17:00; closed Thursdays and Fridays (per official/Tabelog listing; HappyCow lists Thu plus 2nd Friday). Available for private reservations after 17:00 on request. Koji bread baked in-house and sold on Wednesdays and Sundays.

It is set about three minutes east of

chef_bio.background: Café Frosch opened on May 1, 2009, in Kyoto's historic Nishijin textile district, in a renovated traditional machiya (wooden townhouse) about three minutes east of the east gate of Kitano Tenmangu shrine. It was created by two sisters to bring cultural exchange to the historic neighborhood.
chef_bio.philosophy: The café describes itself as a place 'without boundaries' — a space where people of any nationality or age can freely come together to enjoy culture and art. It emphasizes natural ingredients, locally grown Kyoto vegetables, and naturally fermented bread, and welcomes plant-based diners.
chef_bio.specialty: House-baked bread made with whole-grain flour and natural koji yeast — koji bread, bagels, and fig-walnut bread — alongside vegan plates such as a vegan aubergine burger set, koji-bread plates with vegan soup, and an onigiri vegan set. Bread is baked in-house and sold on Wednesdays and Sundays.

anecdotes.text: The café was created as a borderless gathering place for cultural and artistic exchange, hosting events such as English nights, live performances and workshops, and offering rental space.
HappyCow describes it as a café created by two sisters in the historic Nishijin area, combining cultural exchange with vegan-friendly dining and a bakery selling bread on Wednesdays and Sundays.
Its signature bread is risen German-sourdough style using koji, a plant-based fermentation culture, and is made with whole-grain flour and natural yeast.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The café's own Japanese about page confirms the May 1 2009 opening in a Nishijin machiya three minutes east of Kitano Tenmangu's east gate, the borderless culture-and-art concept, and koji bread of whole-grain flour and natural yeast sold Wednesdays and Sundays; HappyCow confirms the two-sister founding and the vegan menu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen is bread-focused, baking with whole-grain wheat flour and koji yeast, so wheat/gluten is pervasive; no gluten-free preparation or separation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is an omnivore kitchen that also serves meat dishes such as a German sausage sandwich, so vegan items are prepared in a shared kitchen; no dedicated vegan-only prep area is documented.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff recommend that you tell them about your vegetarian/vegan needs and any potential allergies before choosing a menu so they can guide your order, and some vegetarian dishes can be modified to remove dairy/eggs.

positives.text: Offers a clearly defined set of vegan dishes — a vegan aubergine burger set, vegan koji-bread and onigiri sets — with plant-based, naturally fermented bread.
Reviewers praise the vegan meals as 'fantastic' with thoughtful meal combinations.

cultural_comfort.note: Founded as a borderless cultural-exchange café with international staff who prepare weekend global dishes, and it hosts English nights, so a foreign student should feel comfortable communicating in English.

places.gf_detail: This is a wheat-udon restaurant — the signature noodles are made from Japanese wheat flour and are not gluten-free. Celiac/strict GF travelers cannot eat the core dishes here.
places.vegan_detail: Omen is an omnivore udon house, but it maintains a dedicated vegan/vegetarian menu available on request. The plant-based set comes with a vegan dashi (fish-free, kelp/vegetable-based dipping broth) instead of the standard bonito dashi, an assortment of fresh and pickled seasonal Kyoto vegetables, ground sesame, and egg-free vegetable tempura. Omen was noted as one of the first noodle shops to explicitly offer a fish-free (vegetarian) dashi. You must ask for the vegan/vegetarian version when ordering, since the default menu is not plant-based.

The name 'Omen' is an honorific dialect word from eastern Japan meaning 'noodles' (men/麺). This Shijo Pontocho branch

chef_bio.background: Omen is one of Kyoto's most beloved udon institutions, with its flagship shop near Ginkaku-ji (the Silver Pavilion) on the Philosopher's Path. The name 'Omen' combines the honorific 'o' with 'men' (麺, noodles). This Shijo Pontocho branch, branded Omen NIPPON, brings the same udon to central Kyoto just off the lively Pontocho lane.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on seasonal Kyoto vegetables and quality domestic wheat, presenting udon as an elegant, vegetable-forward meal rather than a quick noodle bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: Thick, chewy udon made from Japanese wheat, served hot or cold with a dipping tsuyu and a generous spread of seasonal Kyoto vegetables (boiled and pickled) plus freshly ground sesame. The house tsuyu is a fish (bonito-and-kombu) broth; for plant-based diners the kitchen prepares, on request, a vegan version with a fish-free vegetable/kelp dashi and egg-free vegetable tempura.

anecdotes.text: Omen NIPPON keeps a separate vegetarian menu: on request the kitchen prepares a vegan udon with a fish-free vegetable/kelp dashi and vegan (egg-free) vegetable tempura, which reviewers single out for its broth and tempura.

The signature 'omen' set pairs hot or cold udon with a colorful assortment of seasonal Kyoto vegetables such as daikon, gobo, eggplant, greens, ginger and scallions, plus ground sesame to stir into the broth.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Omen.co.jp confirms the Ginkaku-ji flagship and a house broth of Hokkaido kombu and bonito; HappyCow confirms that the Omen NIPPON Pontocho branch offers a request-only vegan udon with a fish-free dashi and egg-free vegetable tempura. The standard broth is fish-based, so the vegan version must be requested.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a wheat-udon kitchen; the noodles, tempura batter and standard tare all contain wheat, so there is heavy gluten presence throughout. No gluten-free preparation or separate handling was described — not suitable for celiac diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No wheat-free soy sauce or tamari was mentioned; the dipping sauce/seasonings should be assumed to contain wheat-based soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The vegan set uses a separately prepared vegan dashi and egg-free tempura, but the kitchen also handles meat and seafood (e.g., prawn tempura). One reviewer reported being mistakenly served the non-vegan version with prawns, so confirm your order.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Vegan/vegetarian orders are accommodated on request with a distinct broth and sides, and an English menu is available, but plant-based is not the default and at least one order mix-up has been reported — communicate your needs clearly.

positives.text: A dedicated vegan/vegetarian set is available with a fish-free (kelp/vegetable) dashi, fresh and pickled seasonal vegetables, ground sesame and egg-free vegetable tempura.
English menu and staff experienced with international visitors make it easy to request the vegan option.

cultural_comfort.note: There is an English menu and the staff are used to international visitors, so a foreign student can order the vegan set comfortably in English — just clearly request the vegetarian/vegan version.

Because South Indian vegetarian cooking commonly uses ghee, yogurt, paneer and dairy, vegan diners should explicitly ask for dairy-free preparation. No published per-dish ghee/dairy breakdown was found, so confirm in person or via Instagram (@indosyokudo_tadka).

A second, more refined dinner location, TADKA2, followed in De

chef_bio.origin: From Aichi Prefecture, Japan; based in Kyoto
chef_bio.background: TADKA's owner-chef, Dai Okonogi (小此木 大), originally from Aichi Prefecture, trained at Mughal, a long-established Indian restaurant in Kyoto, before opening TADKA1 in 2012 as a street-stall-style South Indian lunch spot on Oshikoji-dori. A second, more refined dinner location, TADKA2, followed in December 2021 nearby.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chef travels to India annually to experience regional cooking in homes, temples, street stalls, cafeterias and restaurants, and prizes the 'diversity' of how a single dish changes by region and context. Spice blends are custom-mixed per curry rather than built on a standardized base, and menus rotate daily with what is seasonal and available.
chef_bio.specialty: South Indian 'Meals' (thali-style vegetable set meals) served with rasam, sambar and chutney; weekend morning dosa/tiffin service.

anecdotes.text: TADKA was awarded a Bib Gourmand in the Indian-cuisine category of the Michelin Guide Kyoto 2023.
Roughly three times a year, for South Indian festivals such as Pongal, Vishu and Onam, TADKA serves an all-vegetarian Sadya of about 20 dishes on a banana leaf.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese listings (search-ethnic, Tabelog) identify the owner-chef as 小此木 大 (Dai Okonogi), from Aichi, who trained at the Kyoto Indian restaurant Mughal before opening TADKA in 2012; the official site confirms TADKA1 (Oshikoji-dori lunch) and TADKA2 (Dec 2021 dinner) plus the annual India travel and the ~20-dish banana-leaf Sadya; the Michelin Kyoto 2023 Bib Gourmand is confirmed by Japanese Michelin round-ups.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen also prepares non-vegetarian dishes (especially at the TADKA2 dinner location), so shared cookware/cross-contact is possible; vegan diners should specify dairy-free and meat-free preparation.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Reviewers report the standard menu is vegetarian and that the kitchen will accommodate vegan requests when asked, but no formal allergy protocol is published.

positives.text: The standard daily VEG MEALS set is built from beans and vegetables only (about 9 items), making it an easy, largely plant-based default.
Much of the South Indian repertoire (rice, sambar, rasam, chutney) is naturally wheat-free and based on rice and lentils.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual lunch counter popular with international diners and listed in English-language guides, so basic Japanese helps but you can get by with a few words and pointing at the vegetarian meals set.

Soy sauce (very likely standard wheat-containing) appears in dishes such as the egg-yolk soy sauce yuba rice, and tempura/fried items and seasonings may contain wheat. Yuba and tofu-milk dishes themselves are naturally wheat-free, but cross-use of regular soy sauce and the lack of any stated gluten protocol means a celiac/GF diner must ask directly and cannot assume safety.
places.vegan_detail: This is an omnivore restaurant built around house-made yuba (tofu skin), which is itself plant-based. Many signature elements are vegetable- and soy-forward: the "tofu milk hot pot" with Kyoto vegetables, fresh raw yuba, and yuba-based dishes. However, the kaiseki courses are NOT vegan — they incorporate Miyama-raised Kyoto jidori chicken, free-range egg (e.g. yuba rice topped with egg-yolk soy sauce), and very likely fish-based dashi in soups and seasonings. There is no published dedicated vegan or vegetarian course. A vegan or vegetarian diner would need to phone ahead (075-532-1019) and request a plant-only arrangement; the restaurant explicitly asks for advance notice of allergies and dietary needs, so accommodation may be possible but is not guaranteed. Treat as "ask."
