chef_bio.background: This is the first Kyoto location of くそオヤジ最後のひとふり, a clam-broth ramen brand under Osaka's UNCHI Co., the company behind the celebrated 'Jinrui Mina Menrui' (人類みな麺類). The original Kuso Oyaji opened in Osaka's Juso district in April 2013, and the brand has since reached overseas markets including New York, China, Korea and Nepal. The Kawaramachi-Sanjo shop opened September 15, 2023, set into the Sanjo shopping arcade with a refined Japanese-style interior — counter seats on the first floor and tables on the second (about 19 seats in all).
chef_bio.philosophy: The parent company's stated guiding idea is to 'change the world through the power of ramen,' and the broths are made with custom water-purification equipment to draw out a clean shellfish umami meant to be finished to the last drop.
chef_bio.specialty: Clam-broth ramen, with the あさりラーメン (asari/short-neck clam ramen, around 980–990 yen) as the signature bowl — a clean clam dashi balanced with a blend of dark and light soy sauce, served with chewy yet firm medium-thick straight noodles and clams as a topping. The shijimi (corbicula) and a limited hamaguri (clam) ramen round out the lineup.

anecdotes.text: The Osaka original opened in Juso in April 2013 and the brand has since expanded internationally to New York, China, Korea and Nepal before this first Kyoto outpost.
About a week after opening, an evening visit around 7 PM found roughly ten groups waiting in line — a sign of the strong early buzz around the Kyoto debut.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: PRTimes (UNCHI press release) confirms April 2013 Juso origin, 'change the world through ramen' mission, custom water-purification broth, three clam varieties, ¥980 asari ramen, overseas branches (NY/China/Korea/Nepal) and the Sept 15 2023 Kawaramachi-Sanjo opening. Tabelog confirms 19 seats split 1F counter (10) / 2F tables (9). A local blog notes ~10 groups queuing a week after opening.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are built on a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare — described as a blend of dark and light soy sauce over clam dashi — which typically contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All ramen is shellfish-based (clam dashi with clam toppings); there is no vegan/vegetarian preparation, so cross-contact with shellfish is inherent to the menu.

source_independence.note: This source reprints shop marketing rather than reporting a visit (a curated hub or a press release). It corroborates that a claim was MADE, not that it was verified.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, popular ramen counter where you queue and order at the counter; little English support is expected, so a non-Japanese speaker may want a translated menu or guidance, but pointing at the clam-ramen options works fine.

roles: Operated by the team behind the Osaka-area shop 中華そば ふもと (Fumoto)
chef_bio.background: Yakimeshi to Men Kyoto opened on April 2, 2025 in the Sanjo-meiten-gai arcade just west of Kawaramachi-Sanjo, as a sister shop from the team behind the well-regarded Osaka-area ramen shop Chuka Soba Fumoto (中華そば 麓/ふもと). The concept is right in the name and refreshingly honest: 'we want to eat fried rice AND we want to eat noodles' — so rather than treating the rice as an afterthought side, the shop puts equal craft into both.
chef_bio.philosophy: Take both halves of the classic machi-chuka pairing seriously — neither the noodles nor the rice plays second fiddle. Yuzu powder from Kochi and a grape-sansho (Japanese pepper) oil from Wakayama are set out so diners can tune the bowl to taste, and an evening-only abura soba (oil noodles, from 15:00) gives a different way to enjoy the same house noodles.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the char siu ramen paired with a half portion of fried rice (chashu-men half-yakimeshi set). The bowl is a pork-and-dried-fish double-stock shoyu ramen — pork depth lifted by niboshi (dried sardine) and a finish of shaved bonito — served with house-made straight noodles blending Hokkaido 'yume-chikara' wheat with whole-grain flour, boiled firm. It is crowned with petal-thin rare char siu (pork shoulder loin marinated in a red-wine-and-soy tare). The fried rice is its own point of pride: shredded roast pork and fluffy egg cooked to be moist yet crumbly, with dedicated rice cooked to order per portion.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name literally translates to 'Fried Rice and Noodles,' born from the idea that you shouldn't have to choose between the two — so the half-fried-rice set was made the headline order.
It sits in the Sanjo-meiten-gai arcade and quickly became part of a wave of new ramen shops turning the Sanjo–Kawaramachi blocks into a ramen battleground.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyo-soku and Osumituki confirm the April 2, 2025 opening, that it is run by/sister to Osaka's Chuka Soba Fumoto (麓), the chashu-men half-yakimeshi set, the pork+niboshi+bonito double broth, and house-made Hokkaido 'yumechikara' whole-grain noodles. Kyotopi calls it a sister shop (姉妹店) to Fumoto/Menfu, not a numbered branch. Sources describe the petal-thin rare pork-shoulder char siu in a red-wine soy marinade and yuzu-powder/grape-sansho-oil condiments.

gf_cross_contamination.text: House-made wheat noodles and wheat-based shoyu tare are central to every bowl, and fried rice is cooked on the same line — heavy shared wheat presence throughout the kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen and the char siu is marinated in soy sauce; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat, so the tare and marinade should be assumed to contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is a pork-and-dried-fish (niboshi, bonito) stock and dishes feature pork char siu and egg; no plant-based preparation is mentioned.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, busy arcade ramen shop with no English menu noted; a friendly greeting and pointing at the signature set will carry you through, but staff are unlikely to navigate detailed dietary requests in English.

chef_bio.background: 麺心よし田 is the shop Fushimi locals name first when the talk turns to tsukemen. Tucked just west of Fushimi-Momoyama / Momoyama-Goryomae stations, past the Otesuji shopping arcade, it has built a devoted following over years — regulars describe coming back dozens of times since their student days for noodles that taste reliably the same.
chef_bio.philosophy: The heart of the shop is the house-made noodle — milled from Nagano stone-ground whole-grain flour blended with refined wheat, giving a soba-like fragrance. The kitchen deliberately leaves the cold-rinsed noodles slightly moist, believing that texture carries the wheat aroma best, and serves regular and large portions at the same price.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a rich shrimp tsukemen (海老味噌つけ麺): a dipping broth built from more than a kilogram of sweet-shrimp heads simmered with vegetables, yielding a deep, almost French-bisque-like richness that earns it the nickname of a 'French-inspired' tsukemen. The classic alternative is a chicken-and-seafood (鶏魚介) dip.

anecdotes.text: The shop hands diners a posted 'way of eating' (流儀): start with the noodles as-is, then layer in onion and citrus to shift the flavor in stages, and finish the leftover dip as a consommé-style soup.
The shrimp dip is built from over a kilogram of sweet-shrimp heads, lending the broth its distinctive concentrated, bisque-like body.
A longtime regular writes of having visited dozens of times since student days, praising the unwavering consistency of the bowl.
anecdotes.source: https://minaju.info/lunch/2-16-京都市伏見区-伏見桃山-麺心-よしだ-つけ麺/

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Totteoki Kyoto (official tourism site) confirms the Fushimi-Momoyama/Otesuji location, house noodles from Nagano stone-ground whole-grain flour, the rich shrimp tsukemen built from 1kg+ of sweet-shrimp heads (French-bisque-like), the chicken-seafood dip, the posted 流儀 eating method (noodles first, then onion/citrus, finish the dip as soup), and same-price regular/large portions. A local blog corroborates the devoted-regular following.
sources: https://minaju.info/lunch/2-16-京都市伏見区-伏見桃山-麺心-よしだ-つけ麺/

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locals-beloved counter shop with no English menu noted; basic Japanese and a willingness to follow the posted eating-order instructions will make the visit smooth.

chef_bio.background: Kirin-en opened in 1967, when authentic Cantonese cooking was still a rarity in the then-farmland district of Muko. Founder Miyaji Tamotsu (宮路保) set out to let local residents enjoy genuine Guangdong cuisine casually, and the place has stayed family-run, with Miyaji Ryo (宮路亮) now serving as store manager.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house motto for its spicy dishes is 「辛くて旨い」— 'spicy but delicious' (うま辛) — chasing flavor and craft rather than heat for its own sake.
chef_bio.specialty: A fiery tantanmen built on four kinds of chili plus a house-made meat-miso for depth, which became the restaurant's calling card during Muko City's spicy-food (gekikara) town-revitalization push. In developing it the kitchen reached for the bhut jolokia ('jolokia') pepper — once billed as the world's hottest — and the bowl can be ordered across escalating heat levels (roughly 1 to 5), with the mild steps served without the jolokia powder and the hottest tiers dosed with it.

anecdotes.text: Founded in 1967 by Miyaji Tamotsu to bring real Cantonese cooking to a Muko neighborhood that was still mostly farmland.
The tantanmen earned the Gold Grand Prix at the very first KARA-1 spicy-food competition, the contest run by Muko City's gekikara shopping district.
A quieter favorite is the black-vinegar sweet-and-sour pork (黒酢酢豚), whose depth beneath the tang makes it a regulars' pick.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kirinen.com and the Otokuni-Kyoto guide confirm the 1967 founding by Miyaji Tamotsu (宮路保) with son/manager Miyaji Ryo (宮路亮), authentic Cantonese cooking in then-farmland Muko, the KARA-1 Grand Prix gold-winning tantanmen (four kinds of chili + house meat-miso, bhut/jolokia pepper 'world's hottest at development', selectable 1-5 heat levels), the 「辛くて旨い」うま辛 ethos, and the black-vinegar sweet-and-sour pork.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-noodle tantanmen cooked in shared pots in a Chinese kitchen that also fries and wok-cooks; no gluten-free handling is described anywhere.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a Cantonese restaurant and a tantanmen specialist, dishes rely on standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce and likely wheat-based tare; no wheat-free soy is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Meat- and seafood-forward kitchen with a pork/sesame tantanmen base; no separated vegan prep is indicated.

cultural_comfort.note: A long-running neighborhood Chinese restaurant where Japanese is the working language; a little prepared Japanese or a translation app will smooth ordering, and staff are used to spice-seekers from across Japan.

chef_bio.background: A modest, locally beloved ramen shop in the Nishijin district of Kyoto's Kamigyo ward, set along Chiekoin-dori (知恵光院通) near the old textile quarter. It is the second location (2号店) of Ramen Tengu, whose main shop is in Uzumasa in western Kyoto, and it carries a nostalgic Showa-era chuka-soba feel with a hand-painted sign and a cozy room of wrap-around counter and a few low tatami seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep it simple and let the broth do the work - a clean, comforting Kyoto-style bowl that regulars return for rather than a flashy specialty shop.
chef_bio.specialty: The house bowl, Tengu Ramen, is built on a pork-bone broth blended with Japanese-style dashi: it looks rich and is dressed with back-fat, yet drinks surprisingly clean and stays balanced to the last sip. It comes over thin, springy noodles with menma, nori and a chashu so slow-braised it falls apart and melts on the tongue. A generous heap of fresh, crisp scallions is served on the side so you can pile them in to taste, with an extra-scallion (追いネギ) option for about 50 yen.

anecdotes.text: The chashu is so tender that visitors joke about how many hours it must be simmered - it crumbles apart when lifted with chopsticks and enriches the broth as it dissolves.
The scallions arrive on a separate dish so diners can add as many as they like; an extra-scallions option (追いネギ, ~50 yen) lets you load the bowl up further.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi confirms the Nishijin (Kamigyo) location, that this is the 2号店 with the honten in Uzumasa (Ukyo-ku), the original pork-bone + Japanese-dashi broth that drinks light despite the back-fat, thin broth-clinging noodles with menma and nori, melt-apart chashu, and green onions served separately with a 追いネギ ¥50 add-on.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the broth is a pork-bone/dashi base with a presumed wheat shoyu tare; no gluten-free handling is described.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is described as a shoyu-style (soy-sauce) ramen, which in a shop like this is virtually always a wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are based on animal broth (pork bone plus Japanese dashi) and topped with pork chashu; no vegan or vegetable broth is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, local Nishijin ramen counter where ordering in Japanese and paying cash will go most smoothly; no English service is indicated.

chef_bio.background: Opened in 2002 by a chef who had headed the kitchen (店長／元料理長) at Sugichiyo (杉千代), a legendary Uzumasa ramen shop that drew lines for its then-revolutionary bowls some two decades ago. When Sugichiyo's original shop was gone, Tengu became the refuge for its devoted fans — described as the sole shop carrying Sugichiyo's DNA forward — and it is the original 2002 shop of the Ramen Kyoto Tengu group.
chef_bio.philosophy: Carry the Sugichiyo lineage faithfully rather than chase trends: an honest, additive-conscious pork-bone shoyu bowl in a modest storefront, kept welcoming for families, children and women rather than dressed up as a destination shop.
chef_bio.specialty: Tengu Ramen (てんぐラーメン): a pork-bone and chicken-gara shoyu broth finished with back fat (背脂) that drinks lighter than it looks, paired with thin low-alkaline straight noodles in the Sugichiyo mold and chashu so tender it falls apart when lifted with chopsticks. A basket of chopped green onion is provided to season the bowl to taste, and rice is famously all-you-can-eat.

anecdotes.text: The owner had headed the kitchen at the legendary Sugichiyo and founded Tengu in 2002, becoming the home for orphaned Sugichiyo fans.
The thin low-alkaline straight noodles deliberately mirror Sugichiyo's, and diners are handed a basket of chopped green onion to customize the bowl; the chashu is so soft it crumbles when picked up.
Regulars describe it as carrying on the lineage of the now-gone famous Sugichiyo ramen shop in Uzumasa, with all-you-can-eat rice as a signature touch.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Genjitsutouhi and Retty reviews confirm the Tokiwa (Ukyo-ku) shop was founded in 2002 by a former Sugichiyo (杉千代) head from Uzumasa, that it carries Sugichiyo's 'DNA' as the shop fans turned to, its pork-bone+chicken shoyu broth with back fat, thin low-alkaline Sugichiyo-style noodles, melt-apart chashu, a basket of chopped green onion, and all-you-can-eat rice (ライス食べ放題).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles cooked in a shared boiling pot, plus wheat-wrapped gyoza/shumai/shoronpo on the same line, make gluten cross-contamination unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is a shoyu (soy-sauce) style ramen; Japanese soy sauce almost always contains wheat, so the tare is a wheat source.

chef_bio.background: A small ramen specialist tucked into the Umezu neighborhood of Kyoto's Ukyo ward, on the Arashiyama side of the city near the Hankyu Matsuo-taisha line. The shop has been quietly perfecting one thing for over four decades, opening around 1981 and, in the owner's own words, building it up steadily over roughly 45 years in a corner of Kyoto.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner's stated aim is simple and warm: once a customer comes in, to earn their return and become a shop they patronize for a lifetime - 'a lifelong asset.' Guests are invited to step in without hesitation and give the ramen a try.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a Kyoto-style shoyu ramen in the Daiichi-Asahi (第一旭) mold: a pork clear-broth (tonkotsu seitan) made from Miyazaki-raised pork, seasoned with a light soy-sauce tare. Unlike many Kyoto bowls it skips the heavy back-fat float yet still drinks rich, with a generous layer of oil on top - mild in flavor but satisfyingly hearty. It comes crowned with soft, fatty melt-in-the-mouth chashu, thin bean sprouts, and Kujo green onion over thin, low-hydration straight noodles.

anecdotes.text: The chashu is made from fatty pork sourced from Miyazaki and is so tender it falls apart and melts in the mouth - a detail regulars single out as the highlight of the bowl.
The owner describes the shop as something built up steadily over about 45 years in one corner of Kyoto, and warmly invites newcomers to come in without hesitation and taste it once.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Osumituki (Kyoto ramen guide) places Daiki in Umezu, Ukyo-ku, dates it to roughly 1981 (~36 years as of 2017, i.e. ~45 now), and describes a Daiichi-Asahi-style Kyoto shoyu on Miyazaki pork with an oil float (not heavy back-fat), fatty melt chashu, fine bean sprouts, Kujo negi and thin low-hydration straight noodles. The shop's own site voices the 'lifelong patronage' aim.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, cash-only, counter-only neighborhood shop with no English menu or service; some basic Japanese or pointing at the simple ramen-and-chashu menu will make ordering smooth.

chef_bio.background: Ryumon is widely regarded as one of Kyoto's pioneers of authentic Sichuan cooking, with its original Higashiyama-Sanjo location anchoring a small family of about four branches across the city. The main shop is run with a genuinely Chinese kitchen and floor — Mandarin is spoken throughout, and the cooking balances heat with depth rather than chasing pure spice.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honest, homestyle Sichuan food cooked the way it is in China — real Sichuan chilies and peppercorns, big flavors, late into the night — served in an unpretentious neighborhood setting.
chef_bio.specialty: The scallion-oil chicken noodles (葱油鶏面, ¥650) are the house signature — an inexpensive bowl that regulars describe as authentic enough to bring a tear to your eye. Alongside them, the fiery Sichuan-peppercorn stir-fried eggplant (¥950) and a properly numbing mapo tofu are the dishes locals come back for.

anecdotes.text: The shop draws not only Kyoto locals but visitors from across Japan and even diners from China seeking a taste of home, a marker of how authentic the cooking is.
The dining room is so thoroughly Chinese in feel that one writer joked the inside is 'practically China,' with Mandarin flying between the staff and Sichuan aromatics filling the air.
Regulars single out the 650-yen scallion-oil chicken noodles as 'delicious enough to cry over' and praise it as the real, local flavor.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi and Sotokoto confirm Ryumon as a Kyoto pioneer of authentic Sichuan cooking at Higashiyama-Sanjo (open until ~5am) with roughly four branches, a Chinese kitchen speaking Mandarin, the ¥650 scallion-oil chicken noodles ('泣くほどおいしい'), the Sichuan-peppercorn stir-fried eggplant (¥950), spicy mapo tofu, and diners from across Japan and China. No source states a specific 'Chengdu' style, so that qualifier was removed.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, authentic late-night Chinese spot where Mandarin flies between staff; a little Japanese (or pointing at the menu) goes a long way, and the lively, no-frills atmosphere is welcoming rather than precious.

chef_bio.background: Rosen is a small, calm house restaurant in the Kashihara neighborhood of Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward, a short walk from Hankyu Katsura Station. Owner-chef Fukaya (深谷信人), a Kameoka native, trained from his teens — culinary school, then the celebrated Sichuan restaurant Kato Hanten (華都飯店) that once sat in Kyoto's Holiday Inn, followed by kitchens in Osaka and Nishinomiya — before going solo to Shanghai to study authentic Chinese cooking. He named the shop after Luzhou (瀘州) in Sichuan and opened in Kashihara about a dozen years ago, and he still hand-makes his doubanjiang, tianmianjiang and douchi and cooks with Kashihara- and Kameoka-grown vegetables.
chef_bio.philosophy: Authentic Sichuan and Chinese cooking served generously and affordably in an unfussy, settled space — confident portions and honest pricing rather than show, built on house-made seasonings and local produce.
chef_bio.specialty: Tantan-men is the house signature, offered in white-sesame and black-sesame versions (with a curry tantan-men alongside). The black-sesame bowl is the standout: a rich, deeply aromatic sesame sauce with gentle sweetness and restrained heat over springy noodles — mellow rather than fiercely spicy. The Sichuan mapo tofu comes in mild and tongue-numbing spicy versions, and a salt yakisoba on wide flat noodles finished with a touch of oyster sauce is a quieter favorite.

anecdotes.text: Owner-chef Fukaya, from Kameoka, worked his way through the famed Sichuan restaurant Kato Hanten (華都飯店) and kitchens in Osaka and Nishinomiya, then trained solo in Shanghai, naming the shop for Luzhou (瀘州) in Sichuan.
Lunch sets stay under about 900 yen and the dining room fills at midday, drawn by the fragrant tantan-men and the mapo tofu offered in both mild and tongue-numbing spicy versions.

A reviewer singled out the black-sesame tantan-men for its mellow, sweet-leaning sesame richness and good noodle bounce, and praised the salt yakisoba made with wide flat noodles finished with a touch of oyster sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hankei Kyoto Shimbun profiles owner-chef 深谷信人 (Fukaya, 42, from Kameoka): culinary school from his teens, the Sichuan restaurant Kato Hanten (華都飯店) in the former Kyoto Holiday Inn, then Osaka and Nishinomiya, then solo study in Shanghai; the shop is named for Luzhou (瀘州) in Sichuan, opened ~12 years ago in Kashihara, hand-makes doubanjiang/tianmianjiang/douchi and uses Kashihara/Kameoka vegetables. Kyotopi and Gourpass confirm the white/black-sesame and curry tantan-men (mellow black-sesame standout), mild/spicy Sichuan mapo, salt yakisoba with oyster-sauce finish, and sub-¥900 lunches.

cultural_comfort.note: A neighborhood Chinese restaurant with no indication of English support, so arriving with your order chosen and a few Japanese phrases ready will make things smoothest.

chef_bio.origin: Opened March 2013 in the Nishinokyō neighborhood of Kyoto's Nakagyō Ward, near Nijō Castle and the Sanjō-kai shopping arcade.
chef_bio.background: Owner-chef Shoichi Iwasaki (岩﨑昭一) spent roughly 15 years training at a celebrated tonkotsu ramen shop in Minoh, Osaka — also his hometown — before opening Yoshiharu on March 11, 2013. After leaving the kitchen where he learned his craft, he spent extensive trial-and-error developing the broth that would become the shop's signature.
chef_bio.philosophy: Iwasaki aims for a broth that suppresses the heavy off-odor often associated with pork bone, delivering deep umami and richness with a clean, light finish — a balance of 'umami, richness, and depth.' The shop frames its mission as making ramen — broth, noodles and chashu — that cannot be replicated elsewhere.
chef_bio.specialty: A 'Minoh-style' tonkotsu — distinct from Kyushu tonkotsu — built on a creamy white broth of pork skull and knuckle bones, chicken carcass and chicken feet (momiji), finished with quality back fat, pork skin and plenty of vegetables, then simmered for 24+ hours. The flagship bowl is the special tonkotsu ramen with straight thin noodles, soft sweet chashu, green onion and bean sprouts; the kitchen also offers shoyu, miso, and mayu (burnt-garlic-oil) variations.

anecdotes.text: The shop is regarded as a rarity in Kyoto for being a dedicated pork-bone (tonkotsu) specialist rather than the city's more common lighter styles.
The broth is built from pork skull and knuckle bones plus chicken carcass and chicken feet, back fat, pork skin and vegetables, simmered for 24+ hours.

A favorite move is adding a raw egg to mellow the saltiness, often paired with negi rice.

anecdotes.text: Billed by local food media as Kyoto's first taste of the 'chan-kei' ramen wave that had been spreading through the Kanto region.

chef_bio.background: The owner is a well-known local Jiro-style ramen proprietor long tied to this Fushimi corner on Shidan-dori. Over the years he has run several shops in the area — 'Ramen Dai,' 'Gatts K Ramen,' and 'Ryu no Sakura' — and completed a short training stint at 'Yume o Katare,' the celebrated Jiro-style shop. After stepping away, he returned to the neighborhood, on the spot that once housed 'Ramen Dai,' to open this shop in summer 2024.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop name '夢は力なり' means 'a dream is strength' — an aspirational banner from an owner who left and came back to feed his old neighborhood, carrying the lineage of the Jiro-style shops he trained in and ran before.
chef_bio.specialty: A non-emulsified Jiro bowl: a clean, sharply soy-forward, non-emulsified shoyu broth (rather than the thick cloudy emulsified style), paired with house-made wavy ultra-thick chewy noodles, big chunks of pork, a boiled egg, and a hit of black pepper. Diners customize with the free 'call' system — extra vegetables, oil (abura), and garlic — over generous portions (roughly 300g standard). Aburasoba-style eating is part of the appeal.

anecdotes.text: Local food press framed the 2024 opening as a 'famous proprietor returning' to the ramen-dense Fushimi area, on the corner that once held his earlier shop Ramen Dai.
The broth is described as soy-sharp and clearly defined — a non-emulsified style, distinguishing it from the heavier emulsified Jiro bowls — over self-made thick, wavy, springy noodles.
The owner completed a short training stint at 'Yume o Katare,' a celebrated Jiro-style shop, before returning to run this Fushimi counter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi (kyotopi.jp/articles/l1ige) reports the summer-2024 opening by a well-known local proprietor formerly of Ramen Dai, Gatts K Ramen and Ryu no Sakura, who trained briefly at Yume o Katare; it describes a non-emulsified shoyu Jiro broth, house-made thick wavy noodles, ticket-machine ordering, counter seating and a free topping 'call' system.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are built on pork/pork-bone broth with pork chashu and egg; no plant-based broth or vegan option is offered, so there is no vegan-safe preparation to protect from cross-contact.

chef_bio.background: 鴨町らーめん is a tiny counter-only ramen shop (about nine seats) tucked into the Demachi neighborhood a minute's walk east of Demachiyanagi Station, on a stretch with surprisingly few eateries that makes it a reliable local stop. It has been a fixture of this student-heavy corner of Sakyo Ward, beloved more by neighbors and Kyoto University-area regulars than by tourists.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop sums itself up as 「味よし 麺よし 心よし」 — good taste, good noodles, good heart — and the spirit shows in small touches like complimentary house-made kimchi offered on request and uncooked take-home noodles to enjoy at home.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a mild tonkotsu-shoyu ramen: pork bones and chicken carcasses, carefully cleaned, are simmered for hours with several kinds of aromatic vegetables into a broth that is slightly thick and mellow on the palate, with the pork richness leading over the soy. It is paired with straight medium-thin noodles and fatty, naturally sweet braised chashu. The menu is broad for such a small shop — miso (a blend of several misos), Hakata-style, tantanmen and hearty set meals among them.

anecdotes.text: Regulars and writers single out the hospitality as much as the bowl: the owner and staff are described as approachable and as giving 「丁寧で気持ちがよい接客」 (courteous, pleasant service) — fitting the shop's mellow tonkotsu-shoyu reputation.
Ask and they'll set out free house-made kimchi alongside table condiments like spicy miso and pepper; they also sell uncooked ramen to take home and prepare yourself.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto-gourmet.info and kyotopi (SiMPC) describe a counter-only Demachiyanagi shop with pork-bone-over-soy broth, medium-thin straight noodles, fatty-sweet chashu, free house-made kimchi and take-home noodles; the official site (kamomachi.com) carries the motto 味よし麺よし心よし and confirms a pork-bone/chicken-carcass broth simmered for hours with aromatic vegetables, ~9 counter seats and a miso-blend option.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a tonkotsu-shoyu (pork-bone soy-sauce) base; soy-sauce tare of this kind is virtually always made with wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is simmered from pork bones and chicken carcasses, so all ramen here is animal-based and unsuitable for vegans/vegetarians.

positives.text: Noodles are explicitly egg noodles (たまご麺) — relevant for both egg and wheat allergies.

cultural_comfort.note: A small local counter shop in a student neighborhood with warm, attentive hosts; little to no English is expected, so a few words of Japanese or pointing at the menu will go a long way.

chef_bio.background: こういうもん家 Ro-ji opened on August 5, 2019, tucked down a narrow alley (the "ro-ji" of its name) just south of Demachiyanagi Station. The space was originally a company warehouse, reborn as a half-open, yatai (food-stall) style counter — the kind of hidden-alley spot you stumble onto and feel you've found a secret.
chef_bio.philosophy: A creamy tantanmen tuned to please across age groups rather than to chase extreme spice — approachable comfort food served stall-style, equally happy as a quick lunch or a late-night drinking spot.
chef_bio.specialty: Creamy, mild tantanmen. The house bowl leans on a rich sesame aroma with gentle, not-overpowering heat, topped with ground pork; on request the kitchen will hold back the finishing chili oil (rayu) for milder palates. Variations include a spicy 大辛担々麺, a tomato トマ担麺, and a curry カレー担々麺, and a popular half-size (the local move is to order izakaya snacks first and close the night with a half bowl, or turn the leftover soup into 'tantan rice').

anecdotes.text: Thin noodles are sourced from Kushiro Seimen, a Fushimi-based noodle maker, and served slightly soft; the counter sets out scorched garlic and sansho pepper so you can shift the flavor as you eat.
The shop doubles as a casual izakaya in the evening, with house-made karaage (fried chicken) as a signature side and popular takeout item alongside the noodles.

chef_bio.background: Mimio is a Kyoto institution that spent many years as a beloved late-night, after-drinks ramen haunt in the Gion entertainment district, where it quietly drew a following that included entertainers and professional chefs. In March 2016 it relocated across the city to a quieter spot in Yoshida, Sakyo Ward, near Jingu-Marutamachi, where it carries on the same bowl.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than the usual fast-turnover ramen counter, the owner deliberately designed Mimio as a place to settle in — with counter, tables and a tatami room — so guests can slowly enjoy a drink alongside the bowl. The broth is portioned so you can comfortably finish it to the last sip.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature 名物中華そば is a clear, gentle soy-sauce ramen: a broth drawn carefully from chicken bones and dashi with select ingredients, paired with thin, springy straight noodles and a standout chashu of domestic pork belly sourced from a long-established butcher, simmered until it melts on the tongue. Pidan (century egg) is a popular small plate, and the same broth is even turned into a curry.

anecdotes.text: Before its move, Mimio was a long-loved spot in Gion to cap off a night of drinking, frequented by celebrities and fellow chefs.

chef_bio.background: Menya Kagura opened on February 3, 2021 in the Jodoji / Ginkaku-ji area of Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, taking over the address of Menya Himawari, a beloved salt-ramen shop that had operated there since 2006 before relocating to Shizuoka in November 2020. The new shop is run by the former Himawari owner's brother and opened under the former owner's supervision, carrying the lineage forward in the same little space.
chef_bio.philosophy: A fish-driven ramen specialist standing apart from Kyoto's pork-bone-heavy norm, offering deliberately different lunch (lighter, delicate shio/shoyu) and dinner (richer niboshi) styles from one small counter.
chef_bio.specialty: Niboshi (dried sardine) ramen. The kitchen builds its stock from multiple dried sardines, thick-shaved bonito, kombu, clams and chicken. The signature 濃厚煮干そば is a mild-but-rich niboshi bowl with controlled bitterness and a clean sweetness, while the lighter 淡麗醤油そば and 淡麗塩そば show off fish-forward umami with aromatic chicken oil on top. Medium-thick straight whole-grain wheat noodles from a local noodle maker (麺屋棣鄂) come with generous, well-seared chashu, nori and scallion.

anecdotes.text: The shop sits in the exact former location of Menya Himawari, a salt-ramen shop open since 2006 that moved to Shizuoka in November 2020; Menya Kagura opened there in February 2021 under the former Himawari owner's supervision.

In a Kyoto ramen scene dominated by pork-bone broths, Kagura's dedicated niboshi/seafood focus near Ginkaku-ji and Kyoto University is described as a rare specialty, with the owner running service solo.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny solo-run neighborhood counter shop near Ginkaku-ji where ordering is straightforward but staff likely speak little English; basic Japanese or pointing at the menu goes a long way.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Demachi / north of the Imperial Palace)
chef_bio.background: Biden opened on July 16, 2021, just north of the Kyoto Imperial Palace in the Demachi neighborhood near Demachiyanagi Station, an area with very few ramen shops. The owner had previously cooked at a ramen restaurant over in the Saiin district before striking out on his own. The shop took over the premises of a former izakaya called YAOMON, which had closed after its previous owner fell ill, and Biden kept those izakaya bones — the tatami room and the counter — while reinventing it as a ramen specialist by day.
chef_bio.philosophy: A chicken-paitan style that is rich but elegant, a style the local guides note is rare in Kyoto, served in a relaxed, lived-in room.
chef_bio.specialty: Tori-paitan ramen (around 800 yen): a creamy-looking chicken broth that drinks surprisingly light and refined rather than heavy, paired with straight medium-thin wheat noodles from a long-established Kyoto noodle maker that give the 'patsun' snap locals favor. The bowl is unusually colorful and generous, topped with thin-sliced smoked chicken chashu, chicken tsukune meatballs, sauteed king oyster mushrooms, bell pepper, sweet thick-cut grilled scallions, and daikon sprouts.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a film and arcade-game enthusiast, and the walls of the shop are decorated with movie posters.

The space was a former izakaya (YAOMON) that closed when its previous owner became ill; Biden reused its layout, with tatami seating on one side and the counter and kitchen on the other, and still flips into an izakaya/omakase service in the evenings.
The signature feature is the thick-cut grilled scallion topping, described as a novel touch that turns sweet when chewed.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki.com (160101) confirms the Jul 16, 2021 opening near Demachiyanagi, the owner's prior work at a Saiin ramen shop, the takeover of the former YAOMON izakaya (closed after the owner's illness) keeping tatami and counter, a light-yet-refined ~¥800 tori-paitan with straight medium-thin Kyoto-maker noodles and a colorful topping array, plus the owner's film/arcade posters; kyoto-gourmet.info highlights the thick-cut grilled scallion.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood shop with no indication of English-language service; basic Japanese or a translation app will smooth the visit.

chef_bio.background: 福仙楼 is the 台湾屋台 (Taiwanese street-stall) sibling of the well-known Kitashirakawa ramen shop 東龍, opened on April 30, 2009 along the same stretch of 北白川 and sharing the 第2青山荘 building (both under the parent 有限会社 潜龍). The team studied Taiwanese street-stall noodle cooking and brought that style to this quiet student quarter near Kyoto University of the Arts, running it as a counterpart to 東龍. The two brands have grown deeply intertwined over the years — the 福仙楼そば and 屋台そば bowls have at times been folded into 東龍's own lineup, so its identity as a fully separate shop has blurred; check current status before a visit.
chef_bio.philosophy: Generous, hearty Taiwanese-street-stall-style bowls at student-friendly prices — comfort ramen made to fill you up rather than to chase trends.
chef_bio.specialty: 福仙楼そば — a rich pork-bone-and-chicken broth finished with back fat and a soy (shoyu) tare, poured over medium-thick, flat, straight house-made noodles and crowned with slow-braised tendon and juicy minced Kyotamba heritage pork, plus bean sprouts, scallion and garlic. The menu runs from the base 屋台そば up through larger 福スペシャル and チャーシュー麺 versions that pile on more pork.

anecdotes.text: The shop's identity is rooted in Taiwanese 屋台 (street-stall) cooking: its base bowl is literally called 屋台そば, and the house style was developed by studying Taiwanese street-noodle technique before adapting it to Kyoto.
福仙楼 and 東龍 are sister operations sharing the same 北白川 building, so the creamy 東龍そば and the soy-rich 福仙楼そば trace to steps from each other.

chef_bio.background: The shop sits in the lineage of "Yume Wo Katare Kyoto," the dream-fueled Jiro-style ramen project whose second location in this Senbon-Nakatachiuri neighborhood (Yume Wo Katare Kyoto II) opened on November 29, 2017. True to the Yume Wo Katare ethos, where a location is restructured or reborn under a new name after a set run, the shop was rebranded on April 1, 2025 as あけてもくれても after owner Teru took the whole place over, carrying the same hulking bowls into a new identity.
chef_bio.philosophy: Carry forward the Yume Wo Katare spirit of generous, soul-filling ramen and the discipline of reinventing the shop rather than letting it stagnate, while keeping the experience honest, hands-on, and built around the counter.
chef_bio.specialty: A classic Jiro-style (Ramen Sou-lineage) bowl: ultra-thick, chewy wheat noodles in a sweet soy-and-pork-bone broth, crowned with a fat slab of chashu, a mountain of bean sprouts, back-fat, and garlic. The house also leans into a signature 汁なし (brothless) version, a nod echoed in the playful name.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name, あけてもくれても ("whether it opens or closes / day in, day out"), winks at both its rebirth from Yume Wo Katare and its embrace of the brothless 汁なし bowl.
It traces directly back to Yume Wo Katare Kyoto II, opened November 2017, whose tradition of renaming or restarting a shop after its run led to this April 2025 incarnation under Teru.

chef_bio.background: Mansei is a much-loved old-style neighborhood shokudo (taishoku-do / machi-chuka) in the Nishinokyo–Enmachi area of Kyoto's Nakagyo ward, near Enmachi Station and Hanazono University. It is the kind of culturally-valuable corner eatery (described locally as a 文化財的な街の食堂, a culturally-treasured town diner) that has fed the surrounding neighborhood for generations, with neatly kept food-sample cases in the window, an aged wall menu, manga to read while you wait, and a relaxed table-seat layout. Delivery to local homes and workplaces is part of its everyday rhythm.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honest, affordable, comforting everyday food for the neighborhood — the appeal is the nostalgic, unpretentious shokudo experience rather than any single trend.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the chuka-soba: a simple, body-warming chicken-bone soy (tori-gara shoyu) broth topped with kamaboko fish cake, roast pork, bean sprouts and chopped green onion, served with firm, low-hydration Chinese-style noodles. Beyond the chuka-soba the kitchen turns out a wide home-style range — udon, soba, yakisoba, rice bowls, curry, omurice and stir-fries — at gentle prices, with the tenjoji-don (天とじ丼, egg-bound shrimp-tempura rice bowl, around 680 yen) a noted favorite.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers describe the chuka-soba as a simple, comforting chicken-bone soy broth that seems to soak into your body (シンプルで、身体に染み入る鶏ガラ醤油の中華そば), with kamaboko, roast pork, bean sprouts and green onion over firm, low-hydration noodles.
The shop is praised as a culturally-valuable town diner with carefully kept food samples, a well-aged wall menu and manga to browse, with table seating that encourages a leisurely meal.
The tenjoji-don (天とじ丼) is highlighted: two shrimp tempura and rice enveloped in plenty of dashi-infused egg (海老天ぷら2尾とごはんを出汁を含んだたっぷりの玉子が包み込む), around 680 yen.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi.jp calls Mansei a 文化財的な街の食堂 ('a place we hope stays forever'), with vintage food samples, an aged wall menu, manga/TV, table-only seating, home & workplace delivery, and the 680-yen 天とじ丼 (two shrimp tempura bound in egg over rice); address 京都市中京区西ノ京北壺井町62, near Enmachi/Hanazono University. v-trip.net confirms the chuka-soba's chicken-bone soy broth, kamaboko/roast pork/sprouts/green onion toppings and firm low-hydration noodles, plus a broad shokudo menu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Shared kitchen turning out wheat noodles (udon, soba, ramen, yakisoba), tempura and curry; no gluten-free handling indicated, so high cross-contamination risk for celiac diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The chuka-soba is a chicken-bone soy (shoyu) broth; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat and no gluten-free tare is offered.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths and dishes rely on chicken-bone stock, dashi, pork, fish cake and egg; no vegan preparation indicated.

cultural_comfort.note: A long-standing local neighborhood diner with handwritten/wall menus in Japanese and no English signage indicated, so a little Japanese or pointing at the food samples will smooth the visit.

chef_bio.background: A chicken-broth ramen specialist that opened on July 17, 2023 in the Jujo-Omiya neighborhood of Kyoto's Minami ward (Nishi-Kujo Morimoto-cho), just north of a local yakitori shop and a short walk from Kintetsu Jujo Station. It is described as having been opened by someone who trained at a popular Kyoto chicken-paitan ramen shop near Nishi-Oji.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on the clean umami of chicken - both a light chicken clear broth and a richer chicken paitan - served in a bright, clean, casual room with springy medium-thin straight noodles from the respected Kyoto noodle maker 麺屋棣鄂 (Menya Teigaku).
chef_bio.specialty: Chicken-forward ramen in three styles - tori-shoyu (chicken-soy), tori-shio (chicken-salt) and the signature tori-paitan (creamy chicken broth), plus a mazesoba. anecdotes.text: Opened July 17, 2023 by someone said to come from a popular Kyoto ramen shop, with chicken clear broth and chicken paitan as the signature menu.

The tori-paitan is recommended with negi-mashi (extra scallions, +50 yen); the fresh hand-cut scallions are praised for their sweetness and pleasant bite, over a gentle broth with four slices of chashu and sprouts.

The tori-shoyu uses a sweeter soy tare that pairs well with a light chicken clear broth and bonito dashi, finished with bonito flakes and benina radish sprouts; the half fried-rice set is praised for its fluffy, made-to-order wok-fry.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyo-soku.com and osumituki.com date the opening to 2023-07-17 in Minami-ku's Nishi-Kujo Morimoto-cho, with とり醤油 and とり白湯 as signatures; web search (Tabelog/kyotopi) corroborates the owner previously worked at a popular Nishi-Oji chicken-paitan shop. kyotopi.jp confirms four noodle items (tori-paitan, tori-shio, tori-shoyu, mazesoba), +50-yen hand-cut negi-mashi, four chashu slices, and noodles by テイガク (麺屋棣鄂); noodlers.jp confirms the same 麺屋棣鄂 noodles, the tori-shoyu build (soy tare, chicken clear broth + bonito, benina sprouts) and the made-to-order half fried-rice set.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tori-shoyu bowl is built on a sweet soy-sauce tare, which in Japanese ramen is virtually always wheat-based soy sauce.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual neighborhood ramen counter with no indication of English support, so a few Japanese phrases and pointing at the menu will go a long way.

chef_bio.background: Nakasawa spent about 18 years cooking ramen across Toyama and Tokyo before coming home to open his own shop near Kinkaku-ji in October 2023. By his own account he never set out to be a chef in the abstract — as he puts it, for him there was only ever ramen.
chef_bio.philosophy: He originally planned a clear-broth (chintan) ramen, but mindful of the nearby Ritsumeikan University crowd he reworked it into a creamy-yet-not-overpowering paitan aimed at winning over younger diners. The care shows in details like charcoal-grilled chashu whose smoky aroma carries into the soup — he has been known to ask guests whether they can taste the char.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a chicken-paitan bowl built on a so-called 'quadruple' soup: Kyoto Akaji-dori chicken bones, pork bones, Shinji-ko shijimi clams and a seafood blend (niboshi, scallop, bonito and mackerel), finished with a three-year-aged shoyu tare. The flagship 特製 鶏パイタンらーめん comes with three kinds of chashu (rare pork shoulder, charcoal-grilled belly, thin-sliced loin), a soft-set egg made with Fukuchiyama eggs, and fried enoki mushrooms — a topping the shop bills as rare, possibly a first, in Kyoto.

anecdotes.text: Nakasawa runs the kitchen solo, preparing every bowl himself. A noodle-making machine sits visible from the street, reserved for his plan to eventually make the shop's own noodles in-house; for now the thin straight noodles come from Menya Teigyaku (棣鄂).
The fried enoki topping on the paitan bowl is promoted locally as a Kyoto first, alongside the unusual four-component 'quadruple' broth.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Bowls are dressed with a three-year-aged soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; soy sauce of this type is wheat-based, making the shoyu bowls unsuitable for gluten-free diners.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The single shared broth is an animal stock (chicken, pork, clam, fish); there is no separate vegetarian or vegan preparation, so no bowl can be made vegan.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, friendly solo-run counter shop where a few words of Japanese and a smile go a long way; English support is unlikely, so pointing and basic phrases are the comfortable way to order.

anecdotes.text: The shop carried forward a peppery nira (Chinese chive) side dish inherited from the previous tenant, Ramen Akashin.

Run by two women, the counter is described as welcoming for solo diners, and it is a lunchtime favorite of nearby Kyoto Sangyo University students — fried-chicken (karaage) sets come with generous rice.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki.com confirms Saishin opened 2017-02-19 in Kita-ku's Misonobashi in the premises of Ramen Akashin (closed ~2017-01-19), kept the layout, inherited the taste and a peppery nira side, and serves tori-tonkotsu in shio/shoyu/miso with thicker noodles for miso and thinner for shoyu, near Kamigamo/Kyoto Sangyo University. kyoto-gourmet.info describes it as run by two women (女性2人), welcoming to solo diners, popular with Kyoto Sangyo students, with a pale corn-potage-colored chicken-forward salt broth (~700 yen), medium-thin noodles and one thick charred chashu slice.

chef_bio.background: Shachirin opened on July 15, 2023 on Imadegawa near the Doshisha University campus (about 5 minutes from Imadegawa subway station), bringing the 'Nagoya karamen' style to Kyoto as a branch of the Nagoya brand 名古屋辛麺 鯱輪. The whole 11-seat counter shop leans into its theme — walls, chairs and towels are bright red, as if the room itself were a bowl of spicy ramen.
chef_bio.philosophy: House-developed chili heat built on three kinds of chili pepper blended for sweetness, aroma and spiciness, prepared cup by cup, layered onto a savory umami base.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature is the umami-spicy bowl (旨辛にんにくラーメン) that fuses Nagoya Taiwan-style ramen with Miyazaki karamen: stir-fried minced meat, garlic, Chinese chives, bean sprouts and green onion over noodles, with optional seared chashu and sweet back fat, and a beaten egg to mellow the heat. Diners pick a spice level from normal up through 5 and then several steps beyond, and many pour the leftover spicy soup over a free bowl of rice.

anecdotes.text: The recipe was supervised by Naoto Niiyama (新山直人), head (総大将) of the acclaimed Nagoya ramen shop Menya Hanabi (麺屋はなび), the shop credited with originating Taiwan mazesoba.
The interior is deliberately all-red — walls, chairs and towels — so the whole shop reads as a giant bowl of spicy ramen.
Noodle dishes come with free rice refills, and customers commonly finish by pouring the spicy broth over rice.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: leafkyoto.net confirms the Kyoto Imadegawa branch opened 2023-07-15, the all-red 11-seat room, the 3-chili blend, and roots in the Nagoya brand 名古屋辛麺 鯱輪. Official shachirin.com states the brand's flavor was supervised by 新山直人, the 総大将 of Taiwan-ramen originator 麺屋はなび, and describes the pork/chicken/vegetable base and Nagoya-Taiwan + Miyazaki-karamen fusion; osumituki.com confirms free rice refills.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles in a shared spicy-ramen kitchen; no gluten-free preparation is mentioned (per Leaf Kyoto).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The menu includes a soy-sauce ramen and a chili-based spicy tare; Japanese soy sauce and chili tares are typically wheat-containing, though the page does not list allergens (per Osumituki).

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature bowls are topped with stir-fried minced meat, seared chashu pork, back fat and a beaten egg over a meat broth; no plant-based option is offered (per Leaf Kyoto).

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 11-seat counter ramen bar with no English menu or allergen info; a knowledgeable guide is recommended, though a GF/vegan diner realistically cannot eat here.

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1984 in Kyoto, this counter ramen shop began serving conventional bowls before its owner stumbled onto the idea that would make it world-famous. Working with Kyoto's prized Kujo green onions, he sought a way to keep the noodles screaming-hot while showcasing a mound of fresh raw scallions on top.
chef_bio.philosophy: Treat ramen as both craft and spectacle: preserve traditional Kyoto shoyu ramen flavor while turning each serving into a joyful, memorable performance, and welcome guests from everywhere — the shop states it offers vegan, vegetarian, gluten-free and Muslim-friendly (no-pork) options prepared with the same care.
chef_bio.specialty: Negi Ramen, better known as Fire Ramen: a light yet deeply savory chicken-and-seafood soy-sauce broth piled with fresh Kujo scallions, finished tableside when the cook pours scallion oil heated past 300 degrees Celsius over the bowl. The oil ignites into a column of flame that chars the onions, drawing out their sweetness and aroma while keeping the bowl piping hot.

anecdotes.text: The flames are not just theater: scallion oil heated above 300C throws up a pillar of fire that chars the Kujo onions and keeps the bowl scalding hot. After a 2019 renovation the counter was rebuilt with fire-resistant stainless-steel seating, and staff give a safety briefing and paper aprons before lighting each bowl.

About a year after opening the founder discovered that pouring flaming oil over freshly chopped green onions produced an extraordinary aroma and flavor, and that discovery became the shop's signature Fire Ramen.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official fireramen.com credits founder Masamichi Miyazawa, dates the shop to 1984 near Nijo Castle, describes Fire Ramen's shoyu base and the ~1-year-after-opening discovery of flaming scallion oil, and lists stated vegan/vegetarian/gluten-free/Muslim-friendly options (dietary safety not independently asserted). livejapan.com confirms the 300C+ scallion oil, the flame pillar that chars Kujo scallions, the 2019 stainless-steel renovation, the safety briefing and paper aprons, and the chicken-and-seafood soy broth.

vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: "When you order the vegan menu, a green number card is placed in front of your seat to ensure flawless service for those who have chosen the vegan option."

chef_bio.background: Tucked down a side street just west of Higashioji-dori between Imadegawa and Higashi-ichijo, a short walk from Demachiyanagi and Kyoto University, this little tantanmen counter occupies a space that used to be a neighborhood sake shop with a standing-drink corner. It was reborn in May 2025, reworked under the guidance of Kinshiro (金鵄楼), a Gosho-minami tantanmen specialist that drew lines soon after it opened in 2024.
chef_bio.philosophy: True to its name 'Noodles and Sake' (麺と酒の寅), the place is built around the idea of 'have a drink, then close the night with a bowl of tantanmen' — a casual student-and-local hangout where you tune your own bowl by circling choices on a paper order slip (noodle firmness, scallions, scallion oil, fried onion, meat miso, chili-oil heat, and how much Sichuan pepper).
chef_bio.specialty: Sichuan-style tantanmen in two forms: a rich, creamy soup version and a soup-less (mazesoba-style) version built on thick, flat, crimped wheat noodles that grab the sauce. The flavor leans on a fragrant sesame base lifted by the tingle of Sichuan pepper (huajiao), with a meat-miso topping blended for a deeper, more layered umami than the parent shop.

anecdotes.text: The shop is a Kinshiro-supervised spinoff; rather than copy the parent, it deliberately uses thick flat crimped noodles for the soup-less bowl and a re-blended meat miso to create its own deeper, more complex flavor.

The concept is 'a drink first, then finish with tantanmen' (一杯やって担担麺で〆る), aimed in part at the nearby Kyoto University student crowd, with beef tataki, gyoza, and karaage to go with the sake before the noodles.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi.jp confirms the shop opened May 2025 in a former Yoshida (Sakyo-ku) sake shop with a standing-drink counter near Kyoto University, supervised by Gosho-minami tantanmen specialist 金鵄楼 (Kinshiro, opened 2024, quickly popular); it serves soup and soup-less Sichuan tantanmen with thick flat crimped noodles and a re-blended, more complex meat miso, paper-slip customization (firmness, negi, scallion oil, fried onion, meat miso, chili oil, Sichuan pepper), the '一杯やって担担麺で〆る' concept, ~16 seats, and sides of beef tataki, gyoza and karaage.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, student-friendly local noodle counter where you order by circling options on a paper slip, so basic Japanese (or pointing) makes ordering much smoother; no English service is advertised.

There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, dedicated prep, or allergen handling. Gluten-avoiders should not eat here.
places.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Despite using plant-based (vegetable) oil rather than animal fat, the standard bowl is topped with chashu (pork) and the soy-based tare typically contains animal-derived components. No vegan/vegetarian version is advertised. The "healthier plant oil" framing is a marketing point about fat type, not a plant-based menu. A vegan diner could ask whether a no-chashu bowl is possible, but the tare itself is not confirmed plant-based, so it cannot be recommended as vegan.

chef_bio.origin: 運営は株式会社天輝（油そば味の天徳ブランド、関東発・京都進出）
chef_bio.background: 味の天徳は神奈川（柿生本店）発祥の油そば専門チェーンで、株式会社天輝が運営する。京都には四条木屋町店と祇園店を構え、四条木屋町店は下京区真町、阪急京都河原町駅から徒歩すぐの繁華街にあるカウンター8席ほどの小さな店。
chef_bio.philosophy: 油そばを『第三の麺類』と位置づけ、動物性の脂ではなく植物性の油を使うことでヘルシーさを打ち出している点が京都での売り。客が酢・ラー油で自分好みに仕上げる参加型の一杯。
chef_bio.specialty: 看板は油そば。中太のちょい縮れ麺を醤油ベースのタレと植物油で和えたスープのない一杯で、メンマ・ねぎ・刻み海苔・チャーシューがのる。途中で酢とラー油を加えて味変し『二度美味しい』のが定番の食べ方。醤油だれと塩だれが選べる。

anecdotes.text: 『京都初の油そば専門店』をうたい、植物性の油を使うためあっさり食べられると紹介されている。
途中から酢とラー油を足して二度美味しい、というのが店の定番の食べ方として案内されている。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 株式会社天輝の公式店舗ページで運営会社・神奈川柿生本店発祥・京都四条木屋町/祇園店の存在を確認。Rettyで『途中から酢とラー油を足して二度美味しい油そば』の食べ方を、ぐるぱす等で『京都初の油そば専門店・植物性の油使用』の標榜を確認。店主名は非公開のためnull。

chef_bio.background: A small owner-run Japanese kappo on Tominokoji just north of Shijo in Shimogyo Ward, a few minutes from Kawaramachi. It opened in December 2019 in a space that had previously housed the curry-tsukemen specialist Menya Itadori (麺屋虎杖), which closed at the end of September 2019, and it continues to operate today.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner frames the place around wholehearted Kyoto hospitality (真心込めて、おもてなし) and lively, enjoyable time shared with family and friends ('てら戸でご家族や友人と一緒に賑やかで楽しい時間をお過ごしください').
chef_bio.specialty: By night it is a kappo for sashimi, grilled fish, and sushi paired with sake and shochu; its signature crossover dish is a curry tsukemen whose dipping broth is built on a strong katsuobushi (bonito) dashi so the Japanese dashi flavor holds its own against the sweet, old-soba-shop-style curry, finished with aonori and served with thick noodles, summer vegetables, chicken, and a soft egg.

anecdotes.text: The shop carried on the curry-tsukemen lineage of the address: the previous tenant was Menya Itadori, a curry tsukemen specialty shop that closed on September 30, 2019, and Terado opened the following December offering its own kappo take on the dish.

What makes the bowl distinctive is the deliberate balance of a heavily bonito-forward Japanese dashi against a sweet, aonori-dusted curry, an intentionally kappo-minded reworking of a casual lunch noodle.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイト(ryouriya-terado.com)で店主『寺戸 昌規』と『ご家族や友人と賑やかで楽しい時間を』というもてなしのコンセプトを確認。osumitukiで前テナント麺屋虎杖(2019/9/30閉店)、2019年12月開業、鰹出汁の効いたカレーつけ麺(青のり・夏野菜・鶏・半熟卵)を確認。

chef_bio.origin: Branch of the Osaka-headquartered Roman brand (parent company 株式会社ロマン, founded November 2020, HQ in Higashinari-ku, Osaka), which has grown to more than a dozen locations across Osaka and Kyoto.
chef_bio.background: A Kyoto outpost of the Osaka-born abura soba and maze soba specialist Roman (株式会社ロマン), this shop opened on May 16, 2022 along Imadegawa-dori in the Hyakumanben district, a short walk from Kyoto University. Oil noodles and mixed noodles were still relatively uncommon in Kyoto at the time, which made the new student-friendly counter a notable arrival in the neighborhood.
chef_bio.philosophy: The brand's stated belief is 'シンプルだからこその素材の味を大事にしています' — because the dish is simple, the flavor of the ingredients matters most. That focus shows in the whole-wheat (全粒粉) thick noodles the brand uses for its noodles.
chef_bio.specialty: Abura soba (brothless oil noodles) and maze soba — thick noodles tossed with a special shoyu tare and seasoned oil. The abura soba comes piled with chashu, menma, soft-boiled egg, and nori; the maze soba layers spicy minced meat, chives, green onion, bamboo shoots, and egg yolk over the same noodles. Diners add vinegar and the house chili oil and mix everything vigorously before eating.

anecdotes.text: The shop courts its Kyoto University neighbors directly with a student discount, and noodle portions scale up through 大盛・ダブル・トリプル all the way to a 'challenge' size.

chef_bio.background: The owner trained at the celebrated Kyoto ramen house Raamen Touhichi (らぁ麺とうひち), a Michelin Bib Gourmand name. He went on to serve as manager (店長) at Raamen Suguru (らぁ麺すぐる), then broadened his craft outside ramen at the yakiniku restaurant Nanzan (南山) before opening Minoru on his own on May 18, 2026 in Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku.
chef_bio.philosophy: He values handmade quality, making his own noodles and using domestically sourced ingredients where he can. He is confident enough in the seasoning balance that no table condiments are offered, asking guests to taste the bowl as built.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a rich-yet-mellow tonkotsu-gyokai (pork-bone and seafood) ramen at 1,100 yen with 180g of house-made medium-thick straight noodles, alongside tsukemen at 1,300 yen with 250g of noodles. A special ramen (1,500 yen) tops the bowl with four kinds of chashu made from Niwa Kogen (丹羽高原) pork, plus seasoned egg and extra charred nori.

anecdotes.text: It quickly became one of 2026's talked-about new Kyoto ramen openings, the proprietor opening 満を持して (with great anticipation) after his time at Touhichi.
The L-shaped open-kitchen counter (about 10 seats) gives a live-cooking feel, and the broth shows layered umami — 'ガツンと来る豚の凝縮された旨味' — over a calm, Japanese-style counter with no table condiments.

chef_bio.origin: Takatsuki, Osaka (Kinsei group); Kyoto Station branch
chef_bio.background: Nakamura Shoten is one of the ramen brands of the Kinsei group, founded in Takatsuki, Osaka on November 8, 2001 as 彩色ラーメンきんせい ('colorful ramen Kinsei') — named for the wish to make vividly colored ramen that shines like Venus in the night sky. The group has spent decades refining chicken-and-seafood broths and handmade noodles, and its Nakamura Shoten line carries that work into Kyoto. This branch sits on the 10th-floor Ramen Koji of the Kyoto Station Building.
chef_bio.philosophy: The group builds each bowl around a carefully balanced broth and handmade noodles, with a stated aim of bringing smiles and comfort through a single bowl of ramen ('ラーメンで笑顔に').
chef_bio.specialty: 金の塩 ('gold salt') — a clear, golden shio bowl built on chicken umami and Japanese dashi, given a refined ('お上品') presentation. The menu also runs to chicken-forward and chuka soba bowls; this is Takatsuki-style ramen 'where you can fully savor Japan's distinctive dashi'.

anecdotes.text: The parent brand was founded on November 8, 2001 in Takatsuki with the wish to create 'ramen as vividly colored as Venus shining in the night sky' ('夜空に輝く金星のような鮮やかな色のラーメンを創りたい') — the origin of the 'colorful ramen' (彩色) name.
At the group's Takatsuki home, the 金の塩 is praised for a light, clear chicken-bone broth ('あっさり！鶏ガラの旨味がよいですね！') and a refined, 'お上品' presentation — counter-only and queued at lunch.

chef_bio.background: ラーメン まきさだは、烏丸御池からほど近い中京区高倉通二条西入に2026年4月27日にオープンした、京都の創作中華の名店「京中華 牧定」が手がけるラーメン専門店。割烹を思わせる落ち着いたカウンター10席のみの小さな店で、看板の一杯はもともと牧定でまかないとして振る舞われていたネギそばを、ラーメンとして一から再構築したもの。
chef_bio.philosophy: 店主は世代を超えて愛される地域の店を目指している――「幼い頃に親に連れられて来ていた子どもが、大人になって今度は自分の家族を連れて来る。そんなふうに世代を超えて愛され、地域に根付いた店にしたい」と語る。

chef_bio.background: Opened February 7, 2026 in the Nishi-Kamogamo / Omiya-Yakushiyama corner of Kita-ku, taking over a space that had previously housed another ramen shop. It is a small independent counter built around one idea: a Kyoto bowl you could eat every single day.
chef_bio.philosophy: "毎日食べられるラーメン" — ramen you can eat every day. The seasoning is kept gentle on purpose, the chashu is cooked soft so it appeals across all ages, and the noodles are made in-house: medium-thick angular straight noodles at 25% hydration, rested a day, with egg white worked in to push the wheat aroma that Kyoto diners favor.
chef_bio.specialty: The house pork-shoyu ramen. The broth is a pork clear-soup (豚清湯) made from only pork arm meat and back fat — deliberately no pork bone — so it lands light yet rich ("あっさりコクうま"), then seasoned with Goko (五光), a traditional Kyoto soy sauce, for that familiar nostalgic Kyoto sharpness. The signature move is chashu, piled without restraint: the standard Buta-yado Ramen (¥950) carries 150g, and the Buta-yado Chashu-men (¥1,200) goes to a 210g mountain of tender, thinly-sliced pork arm. A lighter Buta-yasumi Ramen (¥700) keeps just 30g for a quieter bowl.

anecdotes.text: The owner names Daiichi Asahi and Ramen Fuji — pillars of old-school Kyoto ramen — as the inspiration for the style, positioning Buta-yado as a torch-carrier for the traditional Kyoto bowl rather than a trend chaser.

The broth is described as evoking nostalgia for Kyoto residents — 'no off-smell or funk, with pork umami, richness and the sharpness of soy' — and regulars flag the chashu portions as a destination for people who simply want a lot of tender pork.

chef_bio.background: 麺屋 月 is a small abura-soba specialist that opened on February 22, 2026 in Kyoto's Shimogamo neighborhood, on Kitaoji-dori near Kyoto Prefectural University in what is a competitive local ramen district. It is an intimate spot of about seven tables seating roughly fourteen guests.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop leans on quality where it counts: the thick noodles come from Menya Teigaku, a venerable Kyoto noodle maker founded in 1931, and the abura-soba is built to be enjoyed first as-is, then re-seasoned partway through with chili oil and vinegar to change the flavor.

chef_bio.philosophy: The broth is a mellow soy flavoring with deep umami — a back-fat 'seabura chaccha' style that stays drinkable rather than heavy ('背脂ちゃっちゃ系だが、そんなに油はきつくない。まろやかな醤油ダシ'), the kind of bowl meant to cap off a night out in Gion.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature is a Kyoto-style back-fat soy-sauce ramen (背脂醤油ラーメン, 'seabura chaccha'): a clean chicken-bone shoyu broth blanketed with pork back-fat, paired with thin, low-hydration straight noodles and chashu (¥700). A 'special' version (¥900) upgrades the chashu, and a chilled ramen appears in summer.

anecdotes.text: Open only about 22:00–01:00 and run entirely by one person from a six-seat counter, the shop typically sells out after roughly 35 bowls, which is why it is called a 'phantom' ramen that is hard to actually catch open.
It moved from Fushimi Ward into the basement of the Gion First Building, and that move plus TV appearances drove its breakout popularity as a late-night/after-drinking ramen.
The bowl became well-known enough that Ace Cook released a cup noodle 'supervised by owner 樹下真一' recreating the shop's signature 背油醤油ラーメン (released Oct 18, 2021).

chef_bio.background: Ayam-YA grew out of a ramen company whose very first shop opened not in Japan but in Seattle. When the team brought the concept home to Japan's hyper-competitive ramen scene, they struggled to draw crowds, until an Indonesian exchange student asked a simple question that changed everything: 'Do you use only chicken?' That was the moment the founders learned that many visitors could not eat ordinary ramen for religious reasons. Determined to let Muslim travelers in Kyoto enjoy a real bowl of Japanese ramen with peace of mind, they reformulated the recipe and pursued halal certification through the Malaysia Halal Corporation. 'Ayam' means 'chicken' in Indonesian and Malay.
chef_bio.philosophy: Make a genuinely delicious Japanese ramen that observant Muslims and curious travelers alike can eat with peace of mind, by keeping the kitchen free of pork and alcohol and building flavor honestly from chicken rather than additives.
chef_bio.specialty: Tori-paitan (rich chicken) ramen served as the basic shoyu (soy) chicken soba and a richer shio (salt) chicken bowl, with miso also offered; the broths lean on chicken with a seafood aroma for depth, finished with finely minced onion and scallion, and made without chemical seasonings.

anecdotes.text: A turning point came when an Indonesian exchange student asked whether the broth used only chicken, which first made the team aware that some customers could not eat ramen for religious reasons and led them to pursue halal certification.

Owner Saifullah — from Sri Lanka and originally a teacher — came to Japan to study and wished to stay; a devout Muslim, he keeps a prayer space, and the name 'Ayam' is the Indonesian/Malay word for chicken.
The chicken broth carries depth from a seafood aroma, with finely minced onion and scallion adding a herbaceous lift, all achieved without chemical seasonings.

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood machi-chuka (Japanese-style Chinese) restaurant that has fed the Nishikyogoku district for roughly 40 years, just east of Hankyu Nishikyogoku Station on Hanayacho-dori. It draws a cross-section of locals, from solo diners on their lunch break to families, in a bright, big-windowed room with a warm, unpretentious feel.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honest, generous, affordable home-style Chinese cooking for the neighborhood — big portions, courteous service, and prices that keep regulars coming back day after day.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the maabo-tenshinhan (mapo Tianjin rice): a fluffy egg over rice blanketed in a generous, glossy mapo sauce. The sauce is built on house-made fermented black bean paste (豆鼓醤) and several chili pastes with ginger and plenty of garlic, given depth by coarsely minced salted fermented black beans (豆鼓の粒) and finished with house chili oil, with finely minced pork for richness — kept addictively savory rather than punishingly hot, served around 1,050 yen with soup and pickles.

anecdotes.text: The maabo-tenshinhan reportedly began life as a staff meal (まかない) before customers loved it enough that it became the house signature.
The mapo sauce poured over the Tianjin rice contains minced pork and aromatics but no tofu (豆腐は入っていない), giving it a concentrated, umami-rich punch against the mild egg-and-rice base.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-based machi-chuka kitchen: noodles, gyoza, fried items and sauces share woks, fryers and prep surfaces, so cross-contamination with wheat is effectively unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Chinese-diner cooking here relies on standard soy-based and bean-paste seasonings, which in Japan are wheat-containing; the signature mapo sauce is built on house doubanjiang and chili bean pastes.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork, egg and animal stocks run throughout the menu (mapo sauce, gyoza, fried chicken, fried rice), cooked in shared woks, so no dish can be considered free of animal cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly, at-home neighborhood Chinese diner where a little Japanese (or pointing at the menu) goes a long way; English support is not advertised, so come with basic phrases or this guide.

chef_bio.background: A small, refined Sichuan-leaning Chinese kitchen tucked into a quiet stretch of Nijo-dori just south of the Imperial Palace, opened in 2013 and run single-handedly by its chef-owner. He came up through the produce markets before cooking, and that background shows in his sourcing — a cook with a reliable eye for ingredients who keeps the menu deliberately compact.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep the cooking simple and let quality ingredients carry it — the kind of place where, as one chef put it, everything you order somehow tastes good. Heat is balanced and aromatic rather than punishing.
chef_bio.specialty: Sichuan-style cooking pitched a notch upscale rather than fiery for its own sake: a fragrant tantanmen (the lunchtime dry 汁なし version is especially praised), a mapo tofu where the Sichuan pepper and chili oil are rounded out by the sweetness of the ground pork, plus boiled dumplings and sweet-and-sour pork.

anecdotes.text: Run entirely by one person, so the chef notes service may run slow — part of the charm of a true counter operation.
A fellow Kyoto chef of the same age describes the owner as a former market worker with a trustworthy eye for produce, whose relatively simple cooking nonetheless makes everything taste delicious.
Recognized as a Bib Gourmand selection in the Michelin Guide Kyoto 2023 (Nakagyo-ku Chinese).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles, wheat dumpling skins, and wheat-containing Chinese seasonings (soy/bean pastes) are central to the menu and share a single one-cook wok station; assume heavy gluten cross-contact.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sichuan dishes such as the mapo tofu and the chili/sesame tantanmen tare rely on soy- and fermented-bean-based seasonings that typically contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature dishes use pork and animal-based broth/condiments throughout; no dedicated plant-based prep is indicated, and a single chef cooks everything in shared woks.

positives.text: Tiny 14-seat counter with one attentive chef-owner who takes reservations, so allergy questions can be raised directly when booking — though no formal allergen handling is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run Sichuan counter where one chef cooks everything, so Japanese (or a Japanese-speaking companion) and a prior reservation make for the smoothest visit; come ready to be patient and order in Japanese.

chef_bio.origin: 大阪（人類みな麺類系列）
chef_bio.background: Ramen Daisenso ("Ramen World War") is the Kyoto outpost of the acclaimed Osaka ramen group behind Jinrui Mina Menrui, the much-queued shop that turned shoyu ramen into something theatrical. This branch opened in October 2022 on the first floor of a renovated Kawaramachi building (formerly a sushi restaurant) and marked the group's first move into Kyoto.
chef_bio.philosophy: A noodle-first house: the noodle-making room is visible from the street, signalling pride in house-made noodles, paired with generous service — diners can add up to five chashu slices and get a free half-portion noodle refill (kaedama).
chef_bio.specialty: The flagship bowl is the Kansai-dashi shoyu ramen named 'Pistol' (ピストル) — a clear, light-bodied shoyu broth built on Nagoya Cochin chicken bones and scallop, with deep umami and a faint natural sweetness. The lineup of four soy-based bowls also includes 'Heiwa' (平和), 'Sabita Katana' (錆びた刀, a brothless/soupless shoyu), and 'Jiyu' (自由).

anecdotes.text: The shop names its bowls after evocative wartime-and-peace imagery — 'Pistol,' 'Peace,' 'Rusty Sword,' 'Freedom' — fitting the playful 'Ramen World War' branding of the group.
Its arrival was billed as the Osaka queue-shop's first expansion into Kyoto, opening on 4 October 2022.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the kitchen is built around wheat-based shoyu tare; gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Signature bowls are Kansai-dashi shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen; Japanese shoyu tare is brewed from wheat, so the seasoning base contains gluten.

chef_bio.origin: Osaka (Nishinakajima); brand expanded to Kyoto in 2025
chef_bio.background: This is the Kyoto branch of 人類みな麺類, a tsukemen specialty offshoot of one of Osaka's most famous ramen brands. The original 人類みな麺類 opened in Nishinakajima, Osaka in 2012 and built a reputation for weekend lines of fifty-plus people. The dedicated tsukemen shop launched as a new sub-brand in Osaka's Yodogawa ward in April 2025; this Kyoto-shiyakusho-mae location opened on September 1, 2025 as its second outpost, just steps from Kawaramachi-dori.
chef_bio.philosophy: The brand name 人類みな麺類 — playfully glossed in English as 'Human beings, everybody noodles' — captures founder Matsumura's idea that noodles are something all of humanity shares. The kitchen states its aim plainly: to deliver the highest performance it can currently offer and to keep building the finest shop it can.
chef_bio.specialty: Thick whole-grain wheat dipping noodles served with a rich, mellow pork-bone-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) dipping broth lifted with scallion-oil richness. The signature lineup is three broths — 原点 (the 'origin'), macro, and micro — with noodle portions of 200g, 300g and 400g all at the same price. The Kyoto-only bowl is the 九条ネギつけ麺, finished with fragrant local Kujo green onion. A small pork rice bowl and a finishing-rice option round out the dip.

anecdotes.text: Matsumura has said the name was born when he was a high-schooler: after a part-time shift he went for ramen with friends, warmed his hands on the bowl, and the thought struck him — 'humanity is all noodles' (人類はみな麺類や) — which became the name of his first shop.
The dipping noodles are made extremely long — eaters use scissors at the table to cut them as they go — a hallmark carried over from the tsukemen brand.
The Kyoto-exclusive 九条ネギ tsukemen was announced as the local-only special when the shop opened on September 1, 2025.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, popular tsukemen counter where a few words of Japanese and following the eat-as-you-go rhythm (the noodles are very long and you cut them with scissors at the table) will make ordering smooth.

chef_bio.background: 博多長浜ラーメン みよし opened in 1983 (昭和58年) in Kyoto's Kiyamachi/Sanjo entertainment district and has become an old-school local institution — '京都の人間でその名を知らぬ者はいない' (there is no one in Kyoto who doesn't know its name). For roughly four decades it has carried the same Hakata Nagahama taste, its small open counter running late into the night.
chef_bio.philosophy: A purist, no-frills tonkotsu shop: keep the pork-bone broth going, add nothing unnecessary, and let each diner build their own flavor with the tabletop condiments. Regulars even treat certain moves (like adding pepper or curry powder) as 'forbidden,' and finishing by pouring extra broth over rice is part of the ritual.
chef_bio.specialty: Essentially one bowl done one way: Hakata Nagahama-style tonkotsu ramen — a clean, gently sweet pork-bone broth paired with ultra-thin Hakata straight noodles. Diners customize at the table with around eleven free toppings (beni-shoga pickled ginger, coarse ichimi chili, tenkasu tempura scraps, sesame, etc.) and can order kaedama noodle refills, which is treated as part of doing Nagahama ramen 'your way.'

anecdotes.text: Often cited as a place 'everyone in Kyoto knows' (京都の人間でその名を知らぬ者はいない) — an old-establishment late-night ramen counter running since 1983.

Famous celebrity regular: the gourmet entertainer GACKT, who reportedly rarely eats ramen, is said to have been a loyal customer since his university days and to finish with extra broth poured over rice (替えスープ).
Recommended order from fans: ramen with 'barikata' (extra-firm) noodles, customized with beni-shoga, coarse ichimi, and tenkasu — with pepper and curry powder considered the 'forbidden' moves (禁じ手).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core menu is wheat ramen noodles in a shared tonkotsu broth with kaedama (noodle refills), so a single shared noodle/broth workflow — high cross-contamination risk for gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shop is built on a continuously simmered pork-bone broth; there is no separate non-animal broth, so all bowls share an animal-based base.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, retro 16-seat counter-only late-night ramen counter in Kyoto's Kiyamachi nightlife district run by a longtime local family; little to no English, food-ticket ordering, and best approached with basic Japanese and casual ramen-counter etiquette.

chef_bio.philosophy: The whole shop is built around one idea — 毎日でも食べられるラーメン, 'ramen you could eat every day' — leaning on accessible, balanced flavor rather than heavy gimmickry, using selected ingredients like Kyoto Tanba highland pork and Kujo negi.

anecdotes.text: A boiled egg comes with the bowl and a cup of cold matcha is served as an after-meal gesture — small touches that fit the everyday-comfort idea.

It is documented as a 深夜も賑わう地元の繁盛店 — a locally bustling shop that stays busy late, with after-work diners ordering karaage and gyoza alongside an economical fried-rice set, then a last-train crowd queuing outside.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, locals-first neighborhood ramen counter where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will carry you through, though detailed dietary questions in English may be hard.
